citation: 娃斯玛·塔拉提 (Wasima Talati)《唐代于阗王城形制布局初探》,《故宫博物院院刊》2024年第3期
summary: Reviews the debate on the Khotan capital (Grenard/Stein: Yotkan; Shirai: shifting capitals; Huang Wenbi: Ak-sipil, then Melikawat) and reconstructs the Tang royal city from texts and cave murals with Yotkan as its core. Agrees with the study's Yotkan (12.22a).

citation: 新疆维吾尔自治区文物考古研究所等《新疆和田约特干遗址考古勘探报告(2022–2024年)》(launched at the Nov. 2025 symposium 约特干遗址与古于阗国都城研究; publisher not confirmed)
summary: Three seasons of coring and survey at Yotkan, the first systematic fieldwork there since Stein. At the launch, Li Taoyuan argued Yotkan was the 'western city' of a larger Khotan capital. This refines rather than contradicts the study's Yotkan (12.22a). Bibliographic details not yet verified.

citation: Zhang Zhan, Between China and Tibet: A Documentary History of Khotan in the Late Eighth and Early Ninth Century, PhD diss., Harvard University, 2016
summary: Khotanese documents name phęmāña kīṃtha, the 'Fort of Phema' = Chin. 坎城 (Kancheng), seat of the Cira–Six Towns prefecture. Following Stein, Huang Wenbi and Li Yinping 1998, Zhang places it at the Kanaqin (卡那沁) fort near Ulugh-Ziārat, SE of Uzun-Tati, and equates it with Xuanzang's 媲摩. Confirms the study's 12.22.12 with document evidence; also surveys Stein's Domoko-area sites.

citation: 李吟屏《古于阗坎城考》, 马大正、杨镰编《西域考察与研究续编》, 乌鲁木齐: 新疆人民出版社, 1998, 236–262
summary: Identifies the Tang garrison 坎城 (Khot. Kaṃdva, Phema fort) with the ruined fort Kanaqin near Ulugh-Ziārat, reading the Uighur name as a rendering of the Chinese. Supports the study's Uzun-Tati/Ulugh-Ziārat area for 媲摩 (12.22.12). Cited from Zhang 2016; not seen directly.

citation: 文欣《于阗国“六城”(kṣa au)新考》,《西域文史》3 (2008): 109–126
summary: A new study of the Six Towns (Cira, Phaṃña, Birgaṃdara etc.) in the Domoko–Chira area east of Khotan, including their village names. This is the administrative setting of Xuanzang's 媲摩; Phema lay inside the Cira–Six Towns prefecture but was not one of the Six Towns (per Zhang 2016).

citation: 荣新江、文欣《和田新出汉语—于阗语双语木简考释》,《敦煌吐鲁番研究》11 (2008): 45–69; English: Rong Xinjiang & Wen Xin, 'Newly Discovered Chinese-Khotanese Bilingual Tallies', Journal of Inner Asian Art and Archaeology 3 (2009): 99–118
summary: Bilingual tax tallies naming the Six Towns and villages of 7th–8th-c. Khotan, which pin Chinese and Khotanese toponyms to one another. Context for the eastern Khotan places (媲摩, the 六城 villages); no conflict with the study.

An annotated translation of the Tibetan Li yul lung bstan pa, which gives the foundation legends and Tibetan names of Khotan's monasteries (Tsar-ma, So-ma-ña, Ma-ża, Hgum-tir, Gośṛṅga) matching Xuanzang's 毗盧折那, 娑摩若, 麻射 etc. This is the main textual control on the name-based identifications (Chalma-kazān, Somiya, Kum-i-Shahidān) that the study rates low to high.

citation: 朱丽双《敦煌藏文文书〈牛角山授记〉残片的初步研究》,《西域文史》8 (2013): 23–38
summary: A Dunhuang Tibetan fragment of the Gośṛṅga (Ri Glang-ru) prophecy. It bears on the description of 瞿室餕伽山 (12.22.04; study: Kohmāri Hill).

citation: 荣新江、朱丽双《于阗与敦煌》, 兰州: 甘肃教育出版社, 2013 (incl. 朱丽双《于阗教法史》译注, 413–468)
summary: A synthesis of Khotan history and Buddhism from Chinese and Tibetan sources, with a translated Khotanese religious history whose monastery lists parallel Xuanzang's. It is a reference work for Khotan monastery names, not a site-identification study.

citation: 张广达、荣新江《于阗史丛考》(增订本), 北京: 中国人民大学出版社, 2008 (first ed. 上海书店, 1993)
summary: Collected studies on Khotan history, toponymy and administration from Chinese, Khotanese and Tibetan documents. It covers the Tang 毗沙都督府 and the eastern Khotan places. This is the standard Chinese reference behind later location work.

citation: Kumamoto Hiroshi, 'The Khotanese Documents from the Khotan Area', Memoirs of the Research Department of the Toyo Bunko 54 (1996): 27–64
summary: A survey of Khotanese secular documents by findspot (Domoko, Dandan-Uiliq, Mazar-Tagh etc.) and the toponyms they contain. Background for locating Phema and the Six Towns.

citation: 吉田豊『コータン出土8-9世紀のコータン語世俗文書に関する覚え書き』, 神戸: 神戸市外国語大学外国学研究所 (研究叢書38), 2006
summary: Notes on 8th–9th-c. Khotanese secular documents. Among other things, Yoshida identifies Birgaṃdara with Balawaste north of Domoko and treats Six Towns topography. Context for the 媲摩 region; no conflict.

citation: 中日・日中共同尼雅遺跡学術調査隊『日中共同尼雅遺跡学術調査報告書』第1–3巻, 京都, 1996, 1999, 2007 (Chinese ed. 《中日日中共同尼雅遗迹学术调查报告书》)
summary: Survey and excavation of the Niya site (Cad'ota / Han 精絶) in 1988–97, with distribution maps and dating. Occupation ends c. the 4th century. This confirms Niya = 精絶 but raises a dating problem for the study's 12.22.13: Xuanzang's still-inhabited 尼壤城 (c. 644) should lie further south, near the modern Niya oasis, as Stein argued, not at the abandoned desert site. Volume details partly unverified.

citation: 新疆文物考古研究所、日本佛教大学尼雅遗址学术研究机构编《丹丹乌里克遗址——中日共同考察研究报告》, 北京: 文物出版社, 2009 (Japanese ed. 『日中共同ダンダンウイリク遺跡学術調査報告書』, 2007)
summary: Sino-Japanese survey of Dandan-Uiliq (Khot. Gaysāta, Chin. 杰谢), with Wen Xin and Duan Qing on the Khotanese mural inscriptions. Dandan-Uiliq is not one of Xuanzang's named sites; it is background for the Khotan settlement network.

citation: 巫新华、郭物、雷然等《新疆和田地区策勒县达玛沟佛寺遗址发掘报告》,《考古学报》2007年第4期: 489–525
summary: Excavation (2002–06) of Toplukdong 1–2 and Karadong 1 Buddhist shrines at Domoko (Qira county), 6th–8th c., in the Six Towns / Phema district east of Khotan. Gives archaeological context for the 媲摩 area (12.22.12); no direct identification.

citation: 巫新华《新疆和田达玛沟佛寺考古新发现与研究》,《文物》2009年第8期
summary: A summary and interpretation of the Domoko shrine excavations (see wu2007_damagou).

citation: Corinne Debaine-Francfort & Abduressul Idriss (eds.), Keriya, mémoires d'un fleuve: archéologie et civilisation des oasis du Taklamakan, Paris: Fondation EDF / Findakly, 2001
summary: Results of the Sino-French Keriya mission (Karadong, Djoumboulak Koum). Karadong is discussed as a possible seat of Han 扞彌 (Uzun Tati district), the predecessor of 媲摩. Relevant only to the long history of the Keriya delta settlements; not cited in detail here.

citation: 侯杨方《重返帕米尔：追寻玄奘与丝绸之路》, 上海: 上海译文出版社, 2021
summary: Reports GPS-recorded field surveys (from 2013) reconstructing Xuanzang's return route across the Pamirs (波谜罗川, 大龙池, 朅盘陀) and the descent to the plain. Per Fudan field reports, Hou puts 奔穰舍罗 (12.18.05) at Datong township (大同乡), Taxkorgan county, and the 大石崖 (12.18.04) in a concealed valley near Wacha (瓦恰). Both are new candidates beside the study's Kandar Punin / Chichiklik and 'no site'.

citation: 侯杨方《这才是丝绸之路：重抵历史现场的行走》, 北京: 中信出版集团, 2023
summary: A popular-scholarly synthesis of Hou's c. 20 field seasons, including Xuanzang's Pamir route and the Fudan Silk Road GIS. Use it with hou2021_pamir for the route arguments.

citation: 复旦发展研究院 field dispatches of the Fudan Pamir expedition (侯杨方 et al.), April–May 2013
summary: Field dispatches only. They record Hou's proposals: 奔穰舍罗 at Datong township, and 大石崖 at a hidden valley near Wacha, 300+ li SE of Tashkurgan. Cite the books for argument.

citation: 刘屹《玄奘的西行与东归之路再考察》,《光明日报》2025年6月14日, 第10版 (repr. 爱思想 aisixiang.com/data/163842.html)
summary: Takes 波谜罗川 = Great Pamir and 大龙池 = Zorkul (agrees with the study), and 朅盘陀 = Tashkurgan. Argues Xuanzang left the Pamir by the Naiza-tash pass rather than the Payik or Mintaka; that he probably did not pass the 公主堡 (Qiz-qurghan) fort; and that the 大石崖 was off his route. Treats 乌铩 as the Yarkand area (one of the study's two open alternatives).

citation: John Mock, 'Tibetans in Wakhan: New Information on Inscriptions and Rock Art', Revue d'Etudes Tibétaines 36 (2016): 121–141
summary: Field documentation of Old Tibetan inscriptions, mchod rten and rock art along the Afghan Wakhan route Stein followed in 1906. Context for the 8th-c. Tibetan–Tang contest over 護密/Wakhan; not a test of Khandūd (12.15.02).

citation: John Mock, 'Darkot Revisited: New Information on a Tibetan Inscription and mchod rten', Revue d'Etudes Tibétaines 27 (2013)
summary: On the Darkot pass between Wakhan and Yasin/Gilgit, which links Wakhan to the 商彌 (Chitral–Mastuj) region. Tibetan imperial-period evidence only. Pages not verified.

citation: 林立《西域古佛寺——新疆古代地面佛寺研究》, 北京: 科学出版社, 2018. iii+191 pp. ISBN 9787030577696
summary: A typological survey of the surface Buddhist monasteries of Xinjiang, including Subashi (昭怙釐 candidate), Duldur-Aqur, Shikchin (Karashahr) and the Khotan shrines, with dating. The site descriptions are needed to test 01.06.02 and 01.06.04. Bibliographic details from memory; verify.

citation: 庆昭蓉《吐火罗语世俗文献与古代龟兹历史》, 北京: 北京大学出版社, 2017
summary: Tocharian B secular documents (monastic accounts, caravan passes) from Kucha. Discusses Kuchean monastery and place names and their findspots, the documentary basis for any Tocharian name of Subashi or Duldur-Aqur (cf. Pelliot's *coguri for 昭怙釐).

citation: Ogihara Hirotoshi & Ching Chao-jung, 'SI 3656 and other Kuchean tablets related to the Kizil grottoes in the St. Petersburg Collection', Written Monuments of the Orient 2016/2
summary: Tablets linked to the Yurpāṣka monastery (Kizil). Shows that Tocharian monastery names in the Kucha region can be pinned to sites. Not one of Xuanzang's named sites.

citation: 新疆维吾尔自治区文物考古研究所《新疆库车友谊路墓群2025年度考古发掘项目》 (project summary; leader 王永强)
summary: Records a section of the east wall and moat of 龟兹故城 (Pilang) beside the Han–Tang cemetery, with Tang tombs including that of an Anxi deputy protector. Confirms the walled Kucha capital under modern Kuqa (01.06).

citation: Fu, P. & Aguilar de Santana, 'Using GIS and Open Web Resources to Reconstruct Great Tang Records of the Western Regions', AGILE 2019 (Florida International University Digital Commons)
summary: A GIS digitization of 182 Xiyuji place names, with cost-distance validation of the routes. It uses existing identifications and offers no new evidence; useful only as a comparison dataset.

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya & Bakit Amanbaeva (eds.), キルギス共和国チュー川流域の文化遺産の保護と研究 アク・ベシム遺跡、ケン・ブルン遺跡 2011～2014年度. Bishkek/Tokyo: Institute of Cultural Heritage, NAS Kyrgyz Republic & Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties, 2016. 108 pp.
summary: Report of the Tobunken-Kyrgyz seasons 2011-2014 at Ak-Beshim (and Ken-Bulun) in the Chu valley; the site-level basis for the Ak-Beshim = Suyab identification the study already uses (agrees).

citation: Jokura Masayoshi, Yamafuji Masatoshi, Nawabi Yama, Yamauchi Kazuya & Bakit Amanbaeva, 「キルギス共和国アク・ベシム遺跡の発掘（2015年秋期）調査」, WASEDA RILAS JOURNAL 4 (2016): 43-71.
summary: Preliminary report of the autumn 2015 trench in the central Rabat (eastern part) of Ak-Beshim; argues the Rabat is probably the Tang Suiye garrison town (built 679) adjoining the Sogdian Shahristan 1 that Xuanzang saw as 素葉水城; agrees with the study. (Repository under maintenance at download time; no local copy.)

citation: Jokura Masayoshi, Yamafuji Masatoshi, Nawabi Yama, Denda Ikuo, Yamauchi Kazuya & Bakit Amanbaeva, 「キルギス共和国アク・ベシム遺跡の発掘（2015年秋期）調査出土遺物の研究―土器・磚・杜懐宝碑編―」, WASEDA RILAS JOURNAL 5 (2017): 145-175.
summary: Study of the 2015 finds (pottery, bricks) and re-study of the Du Huaibao 杜懐宝 inscription (Anxi vice-protector, 'pacifier of the Ten Names at Suiye'); the epigraphic proof that Ak-Beshim is Tang Suiye = Suyab; agrees.

citation: Jokura Masayoshi, Yamafuji Masatoshi, Nawabi Yama, Denda Ikuo, Yamauchi Kazuya & Bakit Amanbaeva, 「キルギス共和国アク・ベシム遺跡の発掘（2015年秋期）調査出土遺物の研究 ── 土器・瓦編 ──」, WASEDA RILAS JOURNAL 6 (2018): 205-257.
summary: Follow-up Waseda study of the Ak-Beshim (Rabat/Shahristan) material, comparing Rabat strata II-III with late Stratum I of the Shahristan; chronology of the Sogdian town vs Tang fort. Download blocked by Cloudflare; title to be checked.

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya, Kushihara Kōichi & Mochizuki Hidekazu, 「2017年度アク・ベシム遺跡発掘調査報告」, 帝京大学文化財研究所研究報告 17 (2018): 121-168.
summary: Teikyo season 2017 at Ak-Beshim (Shahristan 2 = Tang Suiye fort; tiles of Tang type); supports Ak-Beshim = Suyab/Suiye; agrees.

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya, 「アク・ベシム遺跡第1シャフリスタンの都市プランの変化」, 帝京大学文化財研究所研究報告 18 (2019): 1-17.
summary: Urban-plan phases of Shahristan 1, the Sogdian walled town (5th/6th c. foundation) that matches Xuanzang's 素葉水城 '城周六七里'; agrees.

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya & Bakit Amanbaeva (eds.), Ak-Beshim (Suyab) 2019. Teikyo University Research Institute of Cultural Properties & National Academy of Sciences of the Kyrgyz Republic, 2020.
summary: Season report 2019 (Shahristan 1 and 2); new stratigraphic evidence on the Sogdian city and the Tang garrison; agrees with Ak-Beshim = Suyab.

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya, Kushihara Kōichi, D. Sorokin, Nakayama Chieko & Mochizuki Hidekazu, アク・ベシム（スイヤブ）2016・2017 (帝京大学シルクロード学術調査団調査研究報告1). 帝京大学文化財研究所 / キルギス共和国国立科学アカデミー, 2022. 235 pp. (English/Russian ed.: Amanbaeva & Yamauchi (eds.), Ak-Beshim (Suyab) 2016-2017, 2023, 242 pp.)
summary: Final report of the first Teikyo seasons: Shahristan 2 identified as Tang Suiye fort (679), Shahristan 1 as the Sogdian city; the main post-1985 excavation evidence for 01.07.03; agrees. (Repository down at download time.)

citation: Bakit Amanbaeva & Yamauchi Kazuya (eds.), Ak-Beshim (Suyab) 2018 (帝京大学シルクロード学術調査団調査研究報告). Teikyo University Research Institute of Cultural Properties & Institute of History and Cultural Heritage, NAS Kyrgyz Republic, 2022. 217 pp.
summary: Season 2018 report (Shahristan 2 buildings of the Tang garrison; Shahristan 1); agrees with Ak-Beshim = Suyab. (Repository down at download time.)

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya, Yoshida Yutaka, Uetsuki M., Fujisawa A. et al., アク・べシム（スイヤブ）2022・2023 / Ak-Beshim (Suyab) 2022-2023 (帝京大学シルクロード学術調査団調査研究報告4). 帝京大学文化財研究所・キルギス共和国国立科学アカデミー, 2024. 381 pp.
summary: Seasons 2022-2023 incl. AKB-20/21 (presumed Dayun-si of the Tang town) and Shahristan 1; latest final report on Suyab; agrees.

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya, 「砕葉鎮城の建設とアク・ベシム遺跡シャフリスタン1の都市プランの変化」, 帝京大学文化財研究所研究報告 23 (2025): 255-296.
summary: Argues how the building of the Tang Suiye garrison (679) beside the Sogdian city changed the plan of Shahristan 1; separates the town Xuanzang saw (Shahristan 1) from the later Tang fort; agrees and refines 01.07.03.

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya, 「砕葉鎮城の大雲寺の位置と伽藍配置に関する試論」, 帝京大学文化財研究所研究報告 23 (2025): 167-190.
summary: Proposes the location and plan of the Tang Dayun-si (c. 690s) at Ak-Beshim (AKB-20/21); post-Xuanzang, but confirms the Tang town on the site; agrees.

citation: Saitō Shigeo 齊藤茂雄, 「文献史料から見た砕葉城」, 帝京大学文化財研究所研究報告 21 (2022): 25-37.
summary: Collects the Chinese textual evidence on Suiye/Suyab (Xuanzang, Tang histories, Du Huan) for matching with the excavated Shahristans; agrees.

citation: Yamauchi Kazuya (ed.), Saitō Shigeo, Kakinuma Yōhei & Fukui Jun, 砕葉史研究 (帝京大学シルクロード叢書003). 帝京大学出版会, 2025. 286 pp. ISBN 9784434354212.
summary: Book-length textual history of Suiye/Suyab (Western Turkic seat, Tang garrison, inscriptions); background for 01.07.03; agrees.

citation: L. R. Kyzlasov, 「クズラソフによるアク・ベシム遺跡の発掘」, trans. Yamauchi Kazuya, 帝京大学文化財研究所研究報告 21 (2023): 157-252. (Japanese translation of Kyzlasov 1959.)
summary: Annotated translation of the 1953-54 Soviet excavation report (Buddhist temple, church, Shahristan 1) at Ak-Beshim; useful base for the Suyab identification; agrees.

citation: Yoshida Yutaka 吉田豊, 「帝京大学文化財研究所によるアク・ベシム遺跡（キルギス共和国）の発掘調査について」, 東方学 147 (2024): 94-105.
summary: Overview by a Sogdianist of the Teikyo results incl. Sogdian written finds at Ak-Beshim; confirms the Sogdian character of Suyab (01.07.04 Xuanzang's 窣利 extends to Suyab); agrees.

citation: Fukui Jun 福井淳哉, 「アク・ベシム遺跡およびその近隣出土漢文資料に関する考察―中国史上最西端の文字と文化―」, 大学書道研究 16 (2023).
summary: Re-reads the Chinese inscriptions (Du Huaibao stele etc.) found at and near Ak-Beshim; epigraphic support for Ak-Beshim = Suiye; agrees.

citation: G. L. Semenov (ed.), Суяб. Ак-Бешим [Suyab. Ak-Beshim] (Археологические экспедиции Государственного Эрмитажа). St Petersburg: State Hermitage & Institute of History NAS KR, 2002. 174 pp. (incl. E. I. Lubo-Lesnichenko, 'Сведения китайских письменных источников о Суябе', 115-127.)
summary: Hermitage-Kyrgyz excavations 1996-2001 (church complex, Shahristan 1) and a synthesis of Chinese sources on Suyab; the standard Russian monograph confirming Ak-Beshim = Suyab; agrees.

citation: Antonino Forte, 'An Ancient Chinese Monastery Excavated in Kirgiziya', Central Asiatic Journal 38.1 (1994): 41-57.
summary: Interprets the Du Huaibao inscription and the Tang temple excavated at Ak-Beshim as Chinese Buddhist foundations of Suiye (Dayun-si, 690s); key epigraphic confirmation of Ak-Beshim = Suyab; agrees.

citation: Nurlan Kenzheakhmet 努尔兰·肯加哈买提, 碎叶 (Suiye/Suyab). Shanghai: 上海古籍出版社, 2017.
summary: Chinese monograph on the history and topography of Suyab using Chinese, Turkic and archaeological evidence; supports Ak-Beshim = Suyab (agrees).

citation: Valery A. Kolchenko, 'Buddhism in the Chuy Valley (Kyrgyzstan) in the Middle Ages', trans. Gulzat Usubalieva, [English edition of Kolchenko 2020, 東洋学術研究 59.1: 197-250; venue of English version not verified].
summary: Survey of Buddhist sites at Ak-Beshim (Suyab) and Krasnaya Rechka (Navekat) by the excavator; notes Xuanzang reports no Buddhism at Suyab in 630 and dates the Buddhist monuments to the Tang (Dayun-si) period; agrees with Ak-Beshim = Suyab. (File was already in the folder.)

citation: V. D. Goryacheva & S. Ya. Peregudova, 'Буддийские памятники Киргизии', Вестник древней истории 1996.2: 167-189. (with B. Ya. Staviskii's reply, ibid. 193-195)
summary: Catalogue of the Buddhist monuments of the Chu valley (Ak-Beshim, Krasnaya Rechka, Novopokrovka); context for Suyab; agrees.

citation: V. D. Goryacheva, Городская культура тюркских каганатов на Тянь-Шане (середина VI - начало XIII вв.). Bishkek: KRSU, 2010.
summary: Synthesis of the excavated early-medieval towns of the Chu and Talas valleys (Suyab, Navekat, etc.) under the Turkic qaghanates; background for 01.07.03-01.07.06; agrees with Ak-Beshim = Suyab.

citation: A. I. Torgoev et al., 'The Buddhist Monastery of Krasnaya Rechka Settlement: The Main Findings 2010-2015', in Ch. Baumer & M. Novák (eds.), Urban Cultures of Central Asia from the Bronze Age to the Karakhanids. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 2019, 349-363.
summary: Excavation of the Buddhist monastery at Krasnaya Rechka (Navekat), 40 km W of Ak-Beshim; not a Xuanzang site but fixes the second Chu-valley city so that Suyab is Ak-Beshim; agrees.

citation: Yu Baichuan 于柏川 & Wang Junzheng 王俊铮, 「考古学视野下的唐代“热海道”再探赜——以吉尔吉斯斯坦伊塞克湖南岸为中心」, 考古与文物 2025.4: 126-137.
summary: Survey of 10+ fortified sites (8th-10th c.) on the S shore of Issyk-kul along the Tang 'Rehai road' Kucha-Bedel-Issyk-kul-Suyab; identifies 碎卜戍=Barskoon etc.; supports Xuanzang's route over the Tianshan to the S shore of 大清池 (Bedel side); agrees with Issyk-kul, bears on the 凌山 pass question.

citation: Maxpurat X. Xubbalieva, 'Toponymic Representation of Central Asia in Xuan Zang's "Great Tang Records on the Western Regions"', International Journal of Social Science and Human Research 7.4 (2024): 2516-2520. DOI 10.47191/ijsshr/v7-i04-65.
summary: Short Uzbek survey comparing Xuanzang and Xin Tangshu for Suye, Mingbulak (千泉), Issyk-kul, Muzart; no new evidence; follows standard identifications.

citation: N. V. Aleksandrova (introd., trans., comm.), Записки о западных странах [эпохи] Великой Тан (Да Тан си юй цзи). Moscow: Vostochnaya literatura, 2012.
summary: Russian annotated translation using Soviet/Central Asian archaeology for the identifications of juan 1 (Suyab, Merke, Talas, Chach, Ustrushana, Iron Gate, Termez); a post-1985 commentary to compare with Mizutani/Ji; not checked.

citation: Giles Dawkes, 'Excavating a Silk Road City: the Medieval Citadel of Taraz, Kazakhstan', Archaeology International 16 (2012-2013): 110-119. DOI 10.5334/ai.1603.
summary: UCL-Kazakh excavation in the citadel of Taraz (central market, modern city): medieval stratigraphy from the early medieval period; confirms the old city of Talas/Taraz lies under modern Taraz (ex-Dzhambul); agrees with 01.07.06.

citation: Étienne de la Vaissière, Sogdian Traders: A History, trans. James Ward (Handbook of Oriental Studies 8.10). Leiden: Brill, 2005. (French ed. Histoire des marchands sogdiens, Paris 2002, 2nd ed. 2004.)
summary: Standard history of the Sogdian commercial diaspora incl. the Semirechye colonies (Suyab, Navekat); explains why Xuanzang's 窣利 reaches NE to Suyab; agrees with 01.07.04.

citation: Yoshida Yutaka 吉田豊, 「玄奘とソグド人」, in Chikamoto Kensuke 近本謙介 & Kageyama Etsuko 影山悦子 (eds.), 玄奘三蔵がつなぐ中央アジアと日本. Kyoto: Rinsen, 2023, 33-66.
summary: A Sogdianist's reading of Xuanzang's Sogdian section (names of 窣利 and the Zarafshan principalities, Sogdian forms behind the transcriptions); the most recent philological check of 01.12-01.20; to be read for any changed name-equations.

citation: Kageyama Etsuko 影山悦子, 「玄奘が見たソグド人と「玄奘三蔵絵」のソグド人」, in Chikamoto & Kageyama (eds.), 玄奘三蔵がつなぐ中央アジアと日本, Rinsen, 2023, 341-367.
summary: Art-historical: Sogdians in Xuanzang's text vs the Kamakura picture scroll; no locational argument.

citation: Chikamoto Kensuke & Kageyama Etsuko (eds.), 玄奘三蔵がつなぐ中央アジアと日本. Kyoto: Rinsen, 2023. 370 pp. ISBN 9784653045595.
summary: Collected volume on Xuanzang and Central Asia (incl. Yoshida on Sogdians); check its other chapters for itinerary studies.

citation: Tomoyuki Usami, Alisher Begmatov & Takao Uno, 'Archaeological Excavation and Documentation of Kafir Kala Fortress', Studies in Digital Heritage 1.2 (2017): 785-796. DOI 10.14434/sdh.v1i2.23267.
summary: Japanese-Uzbek excavation at Kafir Kala, SE of Samarkand (proposed = Rivdad, residence of the Samarkand ikhshids, burnt early 8th c.); does not touch the identification of Xuanzang's capital (Afrasiab).

citation: Khodadad Rezakhani, 'Tokharistan and Sogdiana in the Late Sasanian Period', in ReOrienting the Sasanians: East Iran in Late Antiquity. Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 2017.
summary: Political history of Tokharistan and Sogdiana 6th-7th c. (Turks, Hephthalites); context only.

citation: Ching Chao-jung 慶昭蓉, 'Bactria and Tukharistan in Chinese Buddhist scriptures: A case study of three Vibhāṣā texts'. Wiesbaden: Reichert, 2026 (DOI 10.29091/9783752003635/001).
summary: On the extent of Tukharistan vs Bactria/Balkh; reports Kuwayama's (p.c. 2022) and Inaba 2022's narrow Tukharistan (Katagan + Qal'a-ye Zal; between Balkh and Badakhshan), de la Vaissière 2024's separation of Bactria and Tokharistan, Termez's lack of a king (de la Vaissière 2010) and the 29-not-27 polities count (Kuwayama 2020); bears on 01.20.02's extent (study: 'extent varies').

citation: Claude Rapin, Mutalib Khasanov & Shapulat Rakhmanov, 'The Iron Gates Wall near Derbent (Uzbekistan) from Alexander the Great to the 19th century', in Ch. Baumer, M. Novák & S. Rutishauser (eds.), Cultures in Contact: Central Asia as Focus of Trade, Cultural Exchange and Knowledge Transmission (Schriften zur Vorderasiatischen Archäologie). Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 2022, 57-85. ISBN 978-3-447-11880-4.
summary: Franco-Uzbek (MAFOuz-Sogdiane) excavation of the Darband wall in the Shurob valley as the 'Iron Gates' barrier from the 3rd c. BC to the 19th c.; tests where the Iron Gate of the sources lay. The study puts 鐵門 at the Buzgala defile c. 10+ km W of Derbent; check whether Rapin's 'Iron Gates' = the wall pass rather than Buzgala.

citation: Ladislav Stančo, Jan Petřík, Maria Hajnalová, Tatiana Votroubeková & Shapulat Shaydullaev, 'Revising the chronology of the Darband Wall in Central Asia', Antiquity 99.408 (2025): 1586-1603. DOI 10.15184/aqy.2025.10225.
summary: Ten radiocarbon dates for the Darband wall (Shurob valley, between Sarymas and Susiztag): built 3rd c. BC, rebuilt under the Kushans; maps the Bactria-Sogdiana barrier near Derbent; does not discuss Xuanzang or Buzgala. Neutral/compatible with the study.

citation: Ladislav Stančo et al., 'The Iron Gate and its environs in the Hellenistic period: preliminary report', Studia Hercynia 26.2 (2022): 91-114.
summary: Metal-detector survey (629 finds) and a highway section at the Darband wall (Derbent village), four walls, undated; Greek–Kushan framing, no 7th-c. evidence. Not the study's Buzgala defile; does not test Xuanzang's Iron Gate (lit_batch12).

citation: Pierre Leriche & Chakirjan Pidaev, Termez sur Oxus. Cité-capitale d'Asie centrale. Paris: IFEAC / Maisonneuve et Larose (AURORHE 3), 2008. 163 pp., XVI pl.
summary: Synthesis of the Franco-Uzbek excavations at Old Termez and the Buddhist monasteries (Kara Tepe, Fayaz Tepe, Zurmala); confirms Old Termez as the city on the Oxus; reports a 7th-c. epidemic/break in occupation, relevant to Xuanzang's 呾蜜 c. 630 (agrees on site).

citation: Rissho University Uzbekistan Academic Research Group (Ikegami Satoru, Iwamoto Atsushi et al.), Kara Tepe - Buddhist Complex of Termez: Excavation of the Northern Hill 2014-2017. Tokyo: Rissho University, 2020 (English abstracts: Karatepe_abstracts_En.pdf).
summary: Excavation of the Kara Tepe Northern Hill monastery, Old Termez: use from late 1st to 4th c., some rooms to the 6th; bears on whether Xuanzang's '十餘伽藍' at Termez include Kara Tepe; agrees on the site. (Repository down at download time.)

citation: Rissho University, 『ウズベキスタンにおける仏教文化遺産の調査と保護』. Tokyo: Rissho University (Agency for Cultural Affairs project), 2021.
summary: Report on Kara Tepe and the Zurmala stupa (Kanishka-period, radiocarbon late 1st-early 2nd c.) at Termez; Zurmala as the large stupa of Old Termez; agrees on 01.21. (Repository down at download time; file name 『ウズベキスタンにおける仏教文化遺産の調査と保護』.pdf.)

citation: Iwamoto Atsushi, 'Overview of the research of Buddhist sites in Uzbekistan with the cooperation of Rissho University (2014-2021)', Builders of the Future (Tashkent) 2022.
summary: Summary of the Rissho Kara Tepe and Zurmala work; mentions Xuanzang seeing the stupa at Termez (via Strelkov) without discussion.

citation: B. A. Litvinsky & V. S. Solov'ev, 'The Architecture and Art of Kafyr Kala (Early Medieval Tokharistan)', Bulletin of the Asia Institute n.s. 4 (1990): 61-75.
summary: Kafyr-kala (Kolkhozabad, lower Wakhsh valley): fortified palace-town of 7th-8th c. with a Buddhist shrine, the largest early-medieval site of the Wakhsh valley, a candidate seat for Xuanzang's 鑊沙 (study: Wakhsh valley, Kurgan-tyube) or Khuttal; agrees with the valley.

citation: B. A. Litvinskij & T. I. Zejmal', The Buddhist Monastery of Ajina Tepa, Tajikistan: History and Art of Buddhism in Central Asia (Serie Orientale Roma). Rome: IsIAO, 2004.
summary: Final publication of the 7th-8th c. Buddhist monastery near Kurgan-tyube (Wakhsh valley) with the 12 m reclining Buddha; shows Buddhism active in Wakhsh at Xuanzang's time; agrees with 01.26 location.

citation: Hasuike Toshitaka 蓮池利隆, 「2009年タジキスタン方形拝火寺院発掘調査報告」, 新技術開発による文化財保護・修複科学研究 1 (2010): 1-28.
summary: Ryukoku-Tajik excavation of a 7th-c. square fire temple (later Buddhist) in S Tajikistan (site not named on KAKEN; probably Kafyr-kala); religious context of Wakhsh/Khuttal at Xuanzang's time.

citation: 桑山正進「<研究ノート>トハーラの境域と，藍市城と活国都城」『西南アジア研究』91 (2020): 119–132.
summary: Places the capital of 活國 at the town site N of Qal'a-ye Zāl on the S bank of the Amu (after the Life), = Warwālīz of the Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam and the Han 藍市城, not at Kunduz; also counts 29 not 27 Tokharian polities. Already a study source; it is the basis of the study's alternative for 01.28a/12.05.

citation: 桑山正進「バーミヤーン大佛成立にかかわるふたつの道」『東方學報』(京都) 57 (1985): 109–209.
summary: Long study of how the Hindukush route through Bāmiyān came into use and when the colossi were made; includes a section on the 先王伽藍 and the reclining Nirvāṇa image. This is where Kuwayama puts the 臥像 inside the former king's monastery between the colossi, which the study follows for 01.37.02.

citation: 桑山正進「7世紀におけるベグラームの存立」『西南アジア研究』30 (1989): 21–55.
summary: Uses stamped pottery and round towers, and the stratigraphy of Tapa Skandar, to date Begram III down to the 7th c. against Ghirshman's end-date of c. 400. This confirms Foucher's view that Begram was the Kāpiśī capital Xuanzang saw, and rejects Cunningham's Opian. Agrees with 01.38a.

citation: 桑山正進「ガネーシャ神像碑銘にみえるカーブル突厥王の編年」『西南アジア研究』35 (1991): 22–38.
summary: Chronology of the Turk kings of Kabul from the Gardez Gaṇeśa inscription. This is context for the political geography of Kāpiśī and Kabul (弗栗恃薩儻那) after Xuanzang.

citation: 桑山正進「6–8世紀Kapisi–Kabul–Zabulの貨幣と發行者」『東方學報』(京都) 65 (1993): 371–430.
summary: Reclassifies the 6th–8th c. coinages of Kāpiśī, Kabul and Zābul and assigns them to issuers. This bears on the extent and rulers of 迦畢試 and 漕矩吒 (Zābulistān) in Xuanzang's time.

citation: Kuwayama Shōshin, "Historical Notes on Kāpiśī and Kābul in the Sixth–Eighth Centuries", Zinbun 34(1) (1999): 25–77.
summary: Sections on Zhuna and Sūrya, on the Napki coins and the Khingal dynasty of Kāpiśī, and on the shift of power from Kāpiśī to Kabul. The Sūrya cult bears on the 阿路猱山 (Khair Khana) candidate in 01.38.03a, and the Zhuna (蒭那) cult on 漕矩吒. Reprinted in Kuwayama 2002 (already in the project).

citation: 桑山正進 編『慧超往五天竺國傳研究』京都大学人文科学研究所, 1992 (repr. 臨川書店 1998).
summary: Edition and commentary on Hyecho (c. 727). Its commentary on Bāmiyān, Kāpiśī (罽賓), Zābul (謝䫻), Tokharistan (capital 縛底耶), Wakhan (胡蜜) and Shighnan (識匿) gives a second itinerary and Kuwayama's own identifications for many of Xuanzang's places. Comm. nos. 144–145 treat the Tokhara capital (= 活國).

citation: 桑山正進『異相ガンダーラの仏教』(ヒンドゥークシュ南北歴史考古学樷攷 1) 臨川書店, 2022.
summary: Vol. 1 of Kuwayama's collected Japanese papers (all previously uncollected): Buddhism of Gandhāra and Kāpiśī. Likely relevant to the Kāpiśī monasteries; contents not checked.

citation: 桑山正進『新興バーミヤーンの時代』(ヒンドゥークシュ南北歴史考古学樷攷 2) 臨川書店, 2023.
summary: Vol. 2 of the collected papers, on the rise of Bāmiyān. Probably contains the latest form of his views on the colossi, the 先王伽藍 and the reclining image (01.37.02), and on the Bāmiyān–Kāpiśī route. Contents not checked.

citation: 桑山正進『玄奘三蔵の形而下』(ヒンドゥークシュ南北歴史考古学樷攷 3) 臨川書店, 2023. 494 pp.
summary: 19 papers on Xuanzang as the supplier of the material behind the Xiyu ji. They include 「玄奘三蔵の形而下」, 「インドへの道—玄奘とプラバーカラミトラ」, 「玄奘余録—『西域記』『慈恩伝』読後」 and 「玄奘—その旅の環境」. Directly about how far his distances and directions can be trusted as route data.

citation: Kuwayama Shōshin, Collected Articles on Ancient Eastern Afghanistan and Northern Pakistan (ヒンドゥークシュ南北歴史考古学樷攷 4). Kyoto: Rinsen, 2024.
summary: Vol. 4 of the series: his English papers on Kāpiśī, Kabul, Bāmiyān and Gandhāra. Probably overlaps heavily with Kuwayama 2002, which the project already has, so check for papers written after 2002.

citation: 桑山正進「『西域記』『慈恩伝』読後」, in 佐久間秀範・近本謙介・本井牧子 編『玄奘三蔵—新たなる玄奘像をもとめて』勉誠社, 2021.
summary: Kuwayama's reading notes on the Xiyu ji and the Life, comparing the two for route and place data. Reprinted in Kuwayama 2023 (vol. 3).

citation: 宮本亮一「トハーリスターン行政地理研究序説」『東方學報』(京都) 90 (2015): 320–277.
summary: Reconstructs the administrative geography of 7th–8th c. Tokharistan from the Bactrian documents (Rob, Guzgan, Kadagstan, Malr/Madr, Kahmard). It finds that the territory of the khar of Rob roughly matches Xuanzang's 紇露悉泯健 (Rūy + Samangān), so Xuanzang's 國 were real local lordships. Agrees with and supports 01.30 (strengthened).

citation: 宮本亮一「バクトリア語文書中にみえるカダグスタンについて」『東方學報』(京都) 87 (2012): 448–413.
summary: Tests three locations for Bactrian Kadagstan: the Baghlan–Ghori plain (Grenet: Warlu = 活路), the Kunduz plain (the town of Lan in Doc. F) and Taliqan. It discusses Kuwayama's placing of the Sui Tokhara capital, the 活國 capital and Hyecho's 縛底耶 in the Kunduz area. This bears on 活國 (the Lan/藍市 town site) and 縛伽浪; consistent with the study's open alternative.

citation: 宮本亮一「カダグスターンからの手紙」『西南アジア研究』92 (2021): 49–75.
summary: Reads the Bactrian letters sent from Kadagstan (the Baghlan–Kunduz region) for local administration. Context for 活國 and 縛伽浪. An English version is Miyamoto 2023 (BAI 31).

citation: Miyamoto Ryōichi, "Letters from Kadagstan", Bulletin of the Asia Institute n.s. 31 (2023 [2022]): 87–104.
summary: English version of Miyamoto 2021, on the Bactrian letters from Kadagstan. Context for the political units of eastern Tokharistan that Xuanzang lists (活國, 縛伽浪).

citation: 宮本亮一「バクトリア語文書から見たトハーリスターン在地の支配階層」『オリエント』61(1) (2018): 47–57.
summary: Uses the Bactrian documents on the local ruling class of Tokharistan (khār, šao etc.). Background for what Xuanzang's "27 countries" were as political units.

citation: 岩井俊平「トハーリスターンにおける地域間関係の考古学的検討」『西南アジア研究』60 (2004): 1–18.
summary: Compares pottery assemblages of Kushano-Sasanian to early Islamic sites across Tokharistan (north and south of the Oxus) to define regional groups. Archaeological context for the polities Xuanzang lists.

citation: 岩本篤志「トハリスタンの仏教遺跡と玄奘—立正隊による調査をふまえて」『唐代史研究』19 (2016): 256–264.
summary: Relates the Buddhist sites recorded by the Rissho University expedition(s) in northern Afghanistan to Xuanzang's Tokharistan account. It may supply sites for 活國, 縛伽浪 and 紇露悉泯健; not seen.

citation: 岡田理恵子「唐の西域十六都督府はどのように名付けられたのか」『帝京大学文化財研究所研究報告』24 (2026): 113–130.
summary: How the 16 Tang commanderies of 661 in Tokharistan and its neighbours got their names. Their seats (e.g. 月氏都督府 at 阿緩城 = 活國) are evidence for Xuanzang's capitals; not seen.

citation: Étienne de la Vaissière, "Note sur la chronologie du voyage de Xuanzang", Journal asiatique 298(1) (2010): 157–168.
summary: Re-dates Xuanzang's outward journey (departure 629, not 627) from the Turkic events: the death of Tong Yabghu and the murder of Tardu at 活國. The dates fix when he was at Suyab and Huo; no change of location, but the sequence matters for the route.

citation: エチエンヌ・ドゥ・ラ・ヴェシエール (宮本亮一 訳)「玄奘の旅程に関する覚え書き」『帝京大学文化財研究所研究報告』22 (2023): 243–249.
summary: Japanese translation of de la Vaissière 2010 (JA) on the chronology of Xuanzang's journey, published by the Teikyo Ak-Beshim team.

citation: 宮治昭「バーミヤーン西大仏と仏龕壁画—弥勒信仰の生成と玄奘の見聞・信仰」, in 近本・影山 編『玄奘三蔵がつなぐ中央アジアと日本』臨川書店, 2023: 107–186.
summary: Art-historical study of the Western (55 m) Buddha and its niche paintings against Xuanzang's description. Bears on which colossus is the 立佛石像 and which the 鍮石釋迦佛; the study follows the standard pairing (53 m and 35 m).

citation: 「玄奘のコータン来訪とドモコのトプルクトン遺跡」, in 近本・影山 編『玄奘三蔵がつなぐ中央アジアと日本』臨川書店, 2023: 67–104 (author not verified).
summary: Relates Xuanzang's Khotan visit to the Toplukdong temple site at Domoko, in the 媲摩 region E of Khotan. Possible new evidence for 12.22.12 (Uzun-Tati/Ulugh-Ziyārat area); not seen.

citation: Michael Petzet (ed.), The Giant Buddhas of Bamiyan: Safeguarding the Remains. ICOMOS Monuments and Sites XIX. Berlin: Bäßler, 2009.
summary: AMS radiocarbon dates of the clay finish and its timber armature (Blänsdorf et al., pp. 231–35): Eastern (38 m) Buddha 544–595, Western (55 m) 591–644 (2σ), so both most probably stood in c. 630; the polychromy chapter (Blänsdorf, Pfeffer, Melzl, pp. 237–63) finds painted clay, no metal, with gold reported on the Eastern Buddha's bare parts: 鍮石 describes a gold-painted surface. Coded in lit_batch8.

citation: Michael Petzet (ed.), The Giant Buddhas of Bamiyan II: Safeguarding the Remains 2010–2015. ICOMOS Monuments and Sites XXI. Berlin, 2016.
summary: Second ICOMOS report: conservation and further technical study of the niches and fragments. Detail on construction that bears on Xuanzang's description of the two standing Buddhas.

citation: Zémaryalaï (Zamariallai) Tarzi, "Bāmiyān (Afghanistan): récentes fouilles françaises (2002–2006) par la Mission Z. Tarzi", Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres 151(2) (2007): 877–925.
summary: Excavations 2002–06 of the "Monastère oriental" (round the Great Stupa SE of the 38 m Buddha; rebuilt from the later 6th c., burnt 871, so in use in 630) and soundings in the royal city W and SW of the 55 m Buddha (VR 1, VR 2), aimed at Xuanzang's reclining Buddha, not found by 2006; he only locates the "Monastère du roi précédent" between the colossi, after Foucher, and leaves Gholghola open as a second place for the reclining image. Coded in lit_batch8.

citation: Zémaryalaï Tarzi, "Chronique des fouilles du monastère et de la vallée de Bamiyan, entreprises en 2002 et 2003" (Bamiyan: Professor Tarzi's Survey and Excavation Archaeological Mission 2003), The Silk Road 1(2) (2003): 37–39.
summary: Short field report of Tarzi's first seasons, searching for the reclining Buddha at the foot of the cliff E of the 38 m Buddha (Eastern Monastery) and in the royal city.

citation: 東京文化財研究所・名古屋大学博物館 (山内和也 編)『バーミヤーン仏教壁画の編年: 放射性炭素による年代測定』/ Radiocarbon Dating of the Bamiyan Mural Paintings. Tokyo: NRICP, 2006.
summary: AMS dates for the Bāmiyān cave murals, including those of the colossal niches: mostly 5th–9th c., with the Buddha-niche paintings around the 6th–7th c. Gives the chronology of the monasteries Xuanzang describes.

citation: 東京文化財研究所『バーミヤーンにおける考古遺跡の地下探査: 2003年および2005年の調査成果』Tokyo: NRICP, 2006.
summary: Geophysical (GPR and resistivity) survey of buried remains in the Bāmiyān valley in 2003 and 2005, including the zone in front of the Buddha cliff where the 先王伽藍 and the reclining image have been sought.

citation: 東京文化財研究所 文化遺産国際協力センター・アフガニスタン情報文化省『バーミヤーン仏教石窟調査概報』Tokyo, 2008.
summary: Summary report of the Japanese–Afghan survey of the Bāmiyān Buddhist caves (cave inventory, plans). Site context for the monasteries Xuanzang describes.

citation: 森本晋「バーミヤーン谷における考古調査」『奈良文化財研究所紀要』2006: 6–7.
summary: Short report of the Nara National Research Institute's excavation and survey in the Bāmiyān valley (in front of the Eastern Buddha and the cliff), part of the Japanese–UNESCO work.

citation: Deborah E. Klimburg-Salter, The Kingdom of Bāmiyān: Buddhist Art and Culture of the Hindu Kush. Naples–Rome: IUO/IsMEO, 1989 (Series Maior 5).
summary: Standard monograph on Bāmiyān and the related sites (Kakrak, Foladi, Fondukistan), with chronology and the use of Xuanzang's account. Background for the colossi and the Bāmiyān–Kāpiśī route.

citation: Gérard Fussman, Baba Murad, Éric Ollivier, Monuments bouddhiques de la région de Caboul / Kabul Buddhist Monuments. 2 vols. Paris: Collège de France (Publications de l'Institut de civilisation indienne 76), 2008.
summary: Survey of the Buddhist monuments of the Kabul basin (Guldara, Shevaki, Khair Khana, Tepe Maranjan etc.), with route maps. Basic site data for 弗栗恃薩儻那 (12.02) and the Khair Khana candidate for 阿路猱山.

citation: Jean-Claude Gardin et al., Prospections archéologiques en Bactriane orientale (1974–1978). 3 vols. Paris: ERC (Mémoires de la Mission archéologique française en Asie centrale 9), 1989–1998 (vol. 2: B. Lyonnet, Céramique et peuplement, 1997; vol. 3: Description des sites et notes de synthèse, 1998).
summary: Survey of the plains E of the Kunduz river (Dasht-i Qala, Taloqan, Khanabad, Qal'a-ye Zāl zones), with site descriptions and dates. The basic site data for testing a 活國 capital at Qal'a-ye Zāl vs Kunduz, and for 瞢健 (Taliqan–Khanabad) and 阿利尼 (Oxus crossings).

citation: Warwick Ball, Archaeological Gazetteer of Afghanistan, revised edition. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2019.
summary: Revised catalogue of all recorded sites in Afghanistan, with dates and bibliography (e.g. no. 2281 Qal'a-ye Zāl: Kushan to Hephthalite-Turk, 1st–9th c.). The basic tool for checking any site proposed for Xuanzang's places in Afghanistan.

citation: F. R. Allchin, Warwick Ball, Norman Hammond (eds.), The Archaeology of Afghanistan from Earliest Times to the Timurid Period, new edition. Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 2019.
summary: Updated synthesis, with chapters on the Kushan to Islamic periods, Buddhist sites and Bactria. Background for the Afghan sites.

citation: Paul Bernard, Roland Besenval, Philippe Marquis, "Du « mirage bactrien » aux réalités archéologiques: nouvelles fouilles de la DAFA à Bactres (2004–2005)", CRAI 150(2) (2006): 1175–1248.
summary: First reports of the renewed DAFA excavations at Balkh (Bala Hisar, Tepe Zargaran, the walls). Confirms the city's occupation sequence, which is context for 縛喝 and its monasteries. The Persée PDF is behind a captcha.

citation: Arezou Azad, Sacred Landscape in Medieval Afghanistan: Revisiting the Faḍāʾil-i Balkh. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2013.
summary: Study of the sacred topography of medieval Balkh from the Faḍāʾil-i Balkh, including the memory of the Buddhist Naw Bahār. Bears on the location of 納縛僧伽藍 (study: Nau-bahār, stupa probably Top-i Rustam).

citation: Nicholas Sims-Williams, Bactrian Documents from Northern Afghanistan I: Legal and Economic Documents (Oxford 2000; rev. ed. London: Nour/Khalili 2012); II: Letters and Buddhist Texts (London 2007); III: Plates (2012).
summary: Edition of the c. 150 Bactrian documents (4th–8th c.) from Rob, Samangan, Guzgan and Kadagstan, with the place names (Rob, Samingan, Amber, γαρσιγο, Lan, Kadagstan). The study's identifications for 01.30, 01.33 and 01.36 already rest partly on these (the project has some Sims-Williams).

citation: Nicholas Sims-Williams, "Nouveaux documents bactriens du Guzgan (note d'information)", CRAI 146(3) (2002): 1047–1058, doi:10.3406/crai.2002.22500.
summary: Shows that some Bactrian documents were written in Guzgan; identifies places and rulers of Guzgan (dates from 658/9 on), checked against Persian, Arabic and Chinese sources. Bears on 胡寔健 (Jūzjān) and its capital, and on 鋭秣陀 (Amber/Sar-i pul).

citation: Nicholas Sims-Williams and François de Blois, Studies in the Chronology of the Bactrian Documents from Northern Afghanistan. Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2018.
summary: Fixes the era of the Bactrian documents. This dates the Rob and Guzgan lordships relative to Xuanzang's visit (c. 628–630, 644).

citation: Nicholas Sims-Williams, "Ancient Afghanistan and its invaders: linguistic evidence from the Bactrian documents and inscriptions", in N. Sims-Williams (ed.), Indo-Iranian Languages and Peoples (Proceedings of the British Academy 116), 2002: 225–242.
summary: Overview of the Bactrian evidence for Hephthalite and Turkish rule and for local names in northern Afghanistan. Context for Xuanzang's Tokharistan.

citation: Frantz Grenet, "Regional interaction in Central Asia and Northwest India in the Kidarite and Hephthalite periods", in Sims-Williams (ed.), Indo-Iranian Languages and Peoples (PBA 116), 2002: 203–224.
summary: Synthesis of 4th–7th c. political geography. It proposes that Bactrian Warlu = Chinese 活路 (Baghlan–Ghori plain; p. 215), a point used in the debate on Kadagstan and the 活國 region.

citation: Frantz Grenet, "Nouvelles données sur la localisation des cinq yabghus des Yuezhi: l'arrière-plan politique de l'itinéraire des marchands de Maès Titianos", Journal asiatique 294(2) (2006): 325–341.
summary: Relocates the five Yuezhi yabghu seats using new Bactrian evidence (e.g. Kadagstan, Wakhan). Background for Han–Tang names behind several of Xuanzang's Tokharian states.

citation: 稲葉穣『イスラームの東・中華の西—七〜八世紀の中央アジアを巡って』(京大人文研東方学叢書 13) 臨川書店, 2022.
summary: Seventh–eighth-century Central Asia between the caliphate and Tang, from archaeology, coins and languages. States that 7th-c. Tokharistan in the strict sense lay between Balkh and Badakhshan (p. 38). Written for a general audience but by the specialist.

citation: Michael Alram, Deborah Klimburg-Salter, Minoru Inaba, Matthias Pfisterer (eds.), Coins, Art and Chronology II: The First Millennium C.E. in the Indo-Iranian Borderlands. Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2010.
summary: Conference volume on 4th–9th c. Bactria, Kāpiśī, Kabul and Zābul, with papers by Kuwayama, Inaba ("From Kesar the Kābulšāh…"), de la Vaissière, Grenet, Alram and others. Rulers and chronology of the states Xuanzang lists S of the Hindukush.

citation: Klaus Vondrovec, Coinage of the Iranian Huns and Their Successors from Bactria to Gandhara (4th to 8th century CE). 2 vols. Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2014.
summary: Corpus of Alkhan, Nezak, Hephthalite and Turk coinages with mint attributions (Kāpiśī, Kabul, Zābul, Balkh). Evidence for rulers and centres of 迦畢試, 漕矩吒 and 弗栗恃薩儻那.

citation: Giovanni Verardi and Elio Paparatti, "From early to late Tapa Sardar: a tentative chronology", East and West 55 (2005): 405–444.
summary: Chronology of the Buddhist sanctuary of Tapa Sardar at Ghazni, active in the 7th–8th c. It shows Ghazni had a Buddhist centre in Xuanzang's time, relevant to 鶴悉那 = Ghazni (study: weakened).

citation: Jonathan Lee and Nicholas Sims-Williams, "The antiquities and inscription of Tang-i Safedak", Silk Road Art and Archaeology 9 (2003): 159–184.
summary: Buddhist rock-cut site and Bactrian inscription in the Yakawlang area W of Bāmiyān. This is evidence for Buddhism across the wider Bāmiyān kingdom.

citation: Li Rongxi (tr.), The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions. Berkeley: Numata Center for Buddhist Translation and Research (BDK English Tripiṭaka 79), 1996.
summary: Complete modern English translation (no new identifications; it follows the older equivalents). A citable modern translation alongside Beal and Watters.

citation: Errington, Elizabeth. Charles Masson and the Buddhist Sites of Afghanistan: Explorations, Excavations, Collections 1832–1835. British Museum Research Publication 215. London: British Museum, 2017
summary: Re-edits Masson's unpublished records of the stupas and monasteries around Jalalabad (Darunta, Chahar Bagh/Begram plain, Hadda) and Kabul, with site plans and find lists. Reports the placings of the Nagarahara capital (Masson, Simpson, Mizuno 1970–1); Shah Nasr Ghundai = Masson's Tepe Ashrak; Tepe Khwaja Lahori as a third Dīpaṅkara candidate (Mizuno); Ahin-Posh and Hadda 10 deposits dated by coins. Kapiśa sites described without identifications. Coded in lit_batch9.

citation: Ball, Warwick. Archaeological Gazetteer of Afghanistan / Catalogue des sites archéologiques d'Afghanistan. Revised edition. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2019
summary: Revised site-by-site gazetteer (first ed. 1982) with references for every recorded mound, stupa and cave in Laghman and Nangarhar (Hadda, Ahin Posh, Chahar Bagh, Darunta etc.); a lookup tool for the Lampaka/Nagarahara identifications, not an argument. Consistent with the study.

citation: 桑山正進 Kuwayama Shōshin. 「Shah-ji-ki Dheri主塔の遷變」 Tōhō gakuhō 東方學報 (Kyoto) 67 (1995)
summary: Reconstructs the successive building phases of the main stupa at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri from Spooner's records and relates them to the Chinese descriptions (Song Yun's Queli futu, Xuanzang's Kanishka stupa). Confirms Shah-ji-ki-Dheri as Kanishka's stupa (agrees with 02.04.03); bears on where the Kanishka monastery stood.

citation: 桑山正進 Kuwayama Shōshin. 「アウグストゥス靈廟と大ストゥーパ：車輪状構造の由來」 Tōhō gakuhō 東方學報 70 (1998)
summary: On the origin of the wheel-shaped (spoked) foundation of the great stupas, starting from Shah-ji-ki-Dheri; context for the Kanishka stupa's structure, not its location (no change to 02.04.03).

citation: 桑山正進 Kuwayama Shōshin. 『異相ガンダーラの仏教』（ヒンドゥークシュ南北歴史考古学叢攷 I）. Kyoto: Rinsen shoten 臨川書店, 2022
summary: Collected papers (20 studies) incl. the phases of the Shah-ji-ki-Dheri stupa, Taxila monastery layouts, Hadda (Lalma, Tapa Shotor), the Chinese evidence on Gandhara Buddhism, and a chapter on the confusion of the records on Uddiyana versus the actual geography of its Buddhist sites. Central for 02.04.03 and Swat; check the Uddiyana chapter against 03.01.*.

citation: 内記理 Naiki Satoshi. 書評「桑山正進著『異相ガンダーラの仏教』」 Shirin 史林 107.6 (2024): 651–
summary: Review summarising the contents of Kuwayama 2022 part by part (Shah-ji-ki-Dheri phases, Taxila, Uddiyana records vs. geography); use as a guide to that book.

citation: Errington, Elizabeth. 'Numismatic evidence for dating the "Kaniṣka" reliquary.' Silk Road Art and Archaeology 8 (2002): 101–120
summary: Uses the coins from Spooner's relic chamber to date the deposit of the Shah-ji-ki-Dheri casket later than Kanishka I; questions the casket's date, not the site. Identification of the stupa (02.04.03) stands.

citation: Durrani, Farzand Ali, Ihsan Ali and George Erdosy. 'Seven thousand years of settlement at Peshawar: the Gor Khuttree excavations 1992–93' (preliminary report). Ancient Pakistan 10 (1994–95) [title and pages to verify]
summary: Deep sounding at Gor Khatri (old-city mound of Peshawar) giving an urban sequence back to the early historic period; relevant to Puruṣapura's location (02.04.01a) and to the old Gor Khatri vs. Shah-ji-ki-Dheri question for the Kanishka monastery (02.04.06), but reports no monastery. Consistent with the study (Peshawar; monastery at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri). Citation needs checking. [Catalogue check 2026-11-12: not found. Not found in any catalogue. Ancient Pakistan 10 is cited elsewhere as the Rehman Dheri special issue ('Excavations in the Gomal Valley: Rehman Dheri Report 2'), with Durrani/Ali/Erdosy papers on Rehman Dheri beads and seals; a Gor Khuttree paper by Durrani, Ali and others is cited in one secondary l]

citation: Coningham, Robin and Ihsan Ali (eds). Charsadda: The British-Pakistani Excavations at the Bala Hisar. BAR International Series 1709. Oxford: Archaeopress, 2007
summary: Final report of the 1994–97 Peshawar–Bradford excavations at the Bala Hisar, with the first radiocarbon sequence (from the 2nd millennium BC) and a survey of the surrounding Charsadda mounds; confirms the Bala Hisar complex as the ancient city (Puṣkalāvatī). Agrees with 02.04.09; the mound survey may help test Garrick's Shahr-i-Napursan and Gumbaz/Utmanzai sites.

citation: Ali, Ihsan, Robin Coningham, M.A. Durrani and G.R. Khan. 'Preliminary report of two seasons of archaeological investigations at the Bala Hisar, Charsadda, NWFP, Pakistan.' Ancient Pakistan 12 (1998): 1–34
summary: Interim report of the same project (see coningham_ali2007_charsadda); agrees with Charsadda = Puṣkalāvatī.

citation: 内記理 Naiki Satoshi. 「ガンダーラ地方チャナカ・デリーの丘の歴史」 Tōhō gakuhō 東方學報 90 (2015): 276–(=pp. 244–277 in the PDF)
summary: Re-reads the Kyoto University excavations (Mizuno 1962–64) at Chanaka Dheri, N of Shahbaz Garhi, which Foucher took for the stupa N of Varṣapura: no stupa or Buddhist finds, a two-phase palace-type complex. Agrees with the study (Shahbaz Garhi = Varṣapura; Chanaka Dheri is not the stupa, 02.04.14a unlocated).

citation: Nasim Khan, Muhammad. Treasures from Kashmir Smast (The Earliest Śaiva Monastic Establishment). Peshawar, 2006
summary: Publishes the finds (copper plates, seals, coins, inscriptions) from the Kashmir Smast caves in the Babozai/Sakra hills N of Mardan, a large Śaiva cave sanctuary of the 5th–9th c.; the Kashmir Smast has been proposed as an alternative to Karamar hill for Xuanzang's Bhīmā shrine (02.04.17). Whether this book argues that explicitly is unverified; check.

citation: Falk, Harry. 'A copper plate donation record and some seals from the Kashmir Smast.' Beiträge zur Allgemeinen und Vergleichenden Archäologie 23 (2003): 1–19
summary: Edits a copper plate and seals from the Kashmir Smast cave sanctuary (Mardan) naming its deity and institution; relevant if the cave is tested against Karamar as Xuanzang's Bhīmā shrine (02.04.17). Not verified that Falk makes that identification.

citation: Nasim Khan, Muhammad. The Sacred and the Secular: Investigating the Unique Stupa and Settlement Site of Aziz Dheri, Peshawar Valley, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. 3 vols. Peshawar, 2010
summary: Excavation report of the stupa and town at Aziz Dheri (Shewa, Swabi), between Shahbaz Garhi and Hund on the route Xuanzang followed to Udabhāṇḍa; context for the unlocated stupas of this stretch, no explicit identification with a Xuanzang site known to me.

citation: Nishikawa Kōji 西川幸治 (ed.). Gandhāra 2: Rānīgaṭ — A Buddhist Site in Gandhāra, Pakistan, Surveyed 1983–1992. Kyoto: Kyoto University, 1994 (Japanese and English)
summary: Kyoto University survey/excavation of the large hilltop monastery at Ranigat (N of the Indus–Kabul confluence, near Buner); the site lies in the area of the Mahāsattva and Mahāvana traditions and has been discussed as Aornos; no firm Xuanzang identification. Neutral for the study.

citation: Ali, Ihsan. 'Excavations at Hund on the banks of the Indus: the last capital of Gandhara.' In A. Meadows and P.S. Meadows (eds), The Indus River: Biodiversity, Resources, Humankind. Karachi: Oxford University Press, 1999, 269–283
summary: Interim account of the Peshawar University/Directorate excavations begun in 1996 inside the walled town of Hund (Śāhi-period houses, drains, coins); confirms Hund as Udabhāṇḍapura. Agrees with 02.04.18.

citation: Kimmet, Natasha N. 'What archaeological evidence is there for the Śāhi political center at Hund (Udabhāṇḍapura)?' Sourcebook for the Shahi Kingdoms (FWF project P-31246), Vienna, 2021
summary: Short critical review of the evidence for Hund as Udabhāṇḍapura (inscriptions, excavations 1996–, unpublished results, Hargreaves 1926); agrees with 02.04.18 and notes that the excavations remain unpublished.

citation: Agrawal, Jagannath. 'Some observations on the Hund inscription of the reign of Jayapāla Śāhi, dated 146 (Śāhi era).' Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 1985.2: 177–180
summary: Epigraphic note on a Śāhi inscription from Hund; supports the Śāhi-period importance of Hund (02.04.18).

citation: Filigenzi, Anna. Art and Landscape: Buddhist Rock Sculptures of Late Antique Swat/Uḍḍiyāna. With contributions by Luca M. Olivieri and a note by Peter Rockwell. Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2015 (Denkschriften 462)
summary: Catalogue and maps of c. 200 Buddhist rock sculptures of the 7th–8th c. along paths to Swat's sacred areas, with a section on Xuanzang and the archaeological picture of his time; maps the late Buddhist sacred landscape Xuanzang saw. Supports Swat = Uḍḍiyāna; useful to test the sites around Mingora, Ilam and the upper valley.

citation: Olivieri, Luca Maria. 'Guru Padmasambhava in context: archaeological and historical evidence from Swat/Uddiyana (c. 8th century CE).' Journal of Bhutan Studies 34 (2016): 20–42
summary: Summary by the director of the Italian mission of the archaeology of 7th–8th c. Swat (Barikot, rock sculptures, Udegram) and the Tibetan itineraries (O rgyan pa); discusses Mangalaor/Manglawar and Mingora. Supports Swat = Uḍḍiyāna; relevant to the Mingora vs. Manglawar question for 03.01.01a.

citation: Olivieri, Luca M. 'The itinerary of O rgyan pa in Swat/Uḍḍiyāna (second half of 13th century).' Journal of Asian Civilizations 40, no. 1 (2017): 87–101
summary: Reconstructs O rgyan pa's route through Swat using excavated and surveyed sites as fixed points and locates the temple 'Mangalaor' founded by king Indrabhūti near Manglawar; directly relevant to whether Xuanzang's Mengjieli (03.01.01a) is Mingora or Manglawar. The download returned an HTML page; citation details unverified.

citation: Bibi, Ayesha. 'Buddhism and Buddhist heritage of Uḍiyāna as narrated by Xuanzang.' Ancient Punjab 4 (2016–17): 61–74
summary: Goes through Xuanzang's Uḍḍiyāna chapter with the identifications of Deane, Stein, Tucci and the Italian mission (Mungali = Manglawar per Stein vs. Mingora per Tucci; Ilam; Shankardar etc.); a review, no new evidence. Matches the study's identifications.

citation: Olivieri, Luca M. 'Archaeological evidence for a climatic and agrarian crisis in Swat between 530 and 660: possible effects of the so-called "Late Antique Little Ice Age" (LALIA).' Sourcebook for the Shahi Kingdoms, Vienna, 2020
summary: Barikot stratigraphy shows abandonment and agrarian collapse in Swat c. 530–660, matching Xuanzang's picture of ruined monasteries in Uḍḍiyāna; context, no change to identifications.

citation: Faccenna, Domenico and Piero Spagnesi. Buddhist Architecture in the Swat Valley, Pakistan: Stupas, Viharas, a Dwelling Unit. Lahore: Sang-e-Meel, 2014 (ACT Field School Project Reports and Memoirs, Special Volume)
summary: Architectural corpus of the excavated and surveyed Buddhist sites of Swat (Butkara I, Saidu Sharif, Panr, Amluk-dara, Shankardar, Gumbat, Shnaisha, etc.) with plans and dating; the reference for checking which stupa fits Xuanzang's Uttarasena, Mahāvana, Mayū and Rohitaka stupas. A pre-print is on arca.unive.it (Cloudflare blocked the download).

citation: Callieri, Pierfrancesco. Saidu Sharif I (Swat, Pakistan) 1: The Buddhist Sacred Area. The Monastery. IsMEO Reports and Memoirs 23.1. Rome: IsMEO, 1989
summary: Final report on the monastery at Saidu Sharif I, beside Mingora; chronology of the Buddhist sacred areas near the capital. Context for 03.01.01a (Mingora area).

citation: Faccenna, Domenico. Saidu Sharif I (Swat, Pakistan) 2: The Buddhist Sacred Area. The Stūpa Terrace. IsMEO Reports and Memoirs 23.2. Rome: IsMEO, 2001 (vol. dated 1995)
summary: Final report on the main stupa terrace of Saidu Sharif I near Mingora; dates its use and abandonment, context for the sacred areas around Mengjieli (03.01.01a).

citation: Callieri, P., P. Brocato, A. Filigenzi, M. Nascari and L.M. Olivieri. Bīr-kot-ghwaṇḍai 1990–1992: Preliminary Report on the Excavations of the Italian Archaeological Mission, IsMEO. Supplement 73 to AION 52.4. Naples, 1992
summary: First report of the excavations at Barikot (Bazira/Vajirasthāna), the main urban site of middle Swat; continued in the BKG Interim Reports to 2025. Context for Swat urban sites Xuanzang passed (none in places_B names Barikot directly).

citation: Olivieri, Luca M., with Elisa Iori, Michele Minardi and Marco Pinelli. Vajirasthāna: Archaeology of the Barikot Hilltop (Swat, Pakistan). 3 vols. Rome/Lahore: ISMEO/Sang-e-Meel Publications, 2025 [series: ACT Field School Reports and Memoirs, Special Volume 7; BKG Interim Reports XI — from search snippets, not seen on the title page]
summary: Latest report on the Barikot acropolis and Śāhi temple (Vajirasthāna in a Śāradā inscription of Jayapāla); shows continuity from the 7th c. into the Śāhi period. Context for Swat's urban and temple landscape (Xuanzang's deva temples); repository download blocked.

citation: Olivieri, Luca M. and Massimo Vidale. 'Archaeology and art of Swat (Pakistan): fieldwork reports and studies — Archaeological Map of the Middle Swat Valley (AMSV)' East and West 56.1–3 (2006): 73–150
summary: Systematic site survey of the middle Swat valley (Kandak, Kotah, Ilam slopes, Amluk-dara area, Barikot hinterland) with a gazetteer of Buddhist sites; the base map for testing Ilam (03.01.05) and the stupas S of Mingora. Agrees with Ilam = Mt Ilam.

citation: Callieri, Pierfrancesco. 'Buddhist presence in the urban settlements of Swat, second century BCE to fourth century CE.' In P. Brancaccio and K. Behrendt (eds), Gandharan Buddhism: Archaeology, Art, Texts. Vancouver: UBC Press, 2006, 60–82
summary: Relation of the Buddhist sacred areas to the towns of Swat (Barikot, Udegram, Mingora area); context for the capital Mengjieli (03.01.01a).

citation: Olivieri, Luca M. and Anna Filigenzi. 'On Gandhāran sculptural production from Swat: recent archaeological and chronological data.' In W. Rienjang and P. Stewart (eds), Problems of Chronology in Gandhāran Art. Oxford: Archaeopress, 2018, 71–92 [held: the whole volume (Rienjang & Stewart eds., Problems of Chronology in Gandhāran Art, 2018), from the Internet Archive]
summary: Radiocarbon-backed chronology of Swat's Buddhist sites and workshops (Saidu Sharif, Barikot, Amluk-dara), including the 6th–7th c. decline; context for the state of Swat Buddhism in Xuanzang's time. Volume is open access at Archaeopress.

citation: Rienjang, Wannaporn and Peter Stewart (eds). The Geography of Gandhāran Art. Proceedings of the Second International Workshop of the Gandhāra Connections Project, Oxford, 2018. Oxford: Archaeopress, 2019
summary: Open-access volume on the regional geography of Gandhāran sites (Peshawar valley, Swat, Taxila, Afghanistan); chapters to scan for site identifications in the Xuanzang region.

citation: Casalini, Alice and Luca M. Olivieri. Chapter on the Śāhi temple on the East Terrace of the acropolis at Barikot, Swat (c. 700–1000 CE). In H.P. Ray, S. Kulshreshtha and U. Suvrathan (eds), The Routledge Handbook of Hindu Temples. London: Routledge, 2023 (open access)
summary: Excavated Hindu temple at Barikot; context for the deva temples Xuanzang notes in Uḍḍiyāna; no Xuanzang identification.

citation: 定方晟 Sadakata Akira. 「上軍伝説について」 Indogaku Bukkyōgaku kenkyū 印度學佛教學研究 36.1 (1987): 418–
summary: Textual study of the Uttarasena (上軍王) legend behind Xuanzang's stupa; no location argument (03.01.10 Shankardar unaffected).

citation: Sanderson, Alexis. 'Uḍḍiyāna and Kashmir' (section of 'The Śaiva exegesis of Kashmir'). In D. Goodall and A. Padoux (eds), Mélanges tantriques à la mémoire d'Hélène Brunner. Pondicherry: IFP/EFEO, 2007, 265–269
summary: Textual evidence placing tantric Uḍḍiyāna in Swat, next to Kashmir; supports Swat = Uḍḍiyāna (03.01) against Odisha.

citation: Jettmar, Karl (ed.). Antiquities of Northern Pakistan: Reports and Studies 1. Rock Inscriptions in the Indus Valley. Mainz: von Zabern, 1989 (Text and Plates; with Fussman, von Hinüber, Sander, Sims-Williams, Ma Yong) [held: Text volume only]
summary: Editions of the Kharoṣṭhī, Brāhmī, Sogdian and Chinese rock inscriptions of Chilas, Thalpan, Shatial and Hunza, incl. von Hinüber on Buddhist inscriptions of the upper Indus (Palola rulers) and Ma Yong's Wei envoy inscription; primary evidence for the Indus-gorge route and for Bolor/Darel. Heidelberg's bot check blocked the download.

citation: Jettmar, Karl (ed.). Antiquities of Northern Pakistan 2. Mainz: von Zabern, 1993 (incl. Fussman, 'Chilas, Hatun et les bronzes bouddhiques du Cachemire'; Jettmar, 'The Paṭolas, their governors and their successors'; Höllmann on Chinese inscriptions)

citation: Fussman, Gérard (ed.). Antiquities of Northern Pakistan 3. Mainz: von Zabern, 1994 (Shatial stupa triptych, Chilas-Thalpan and Tibetan art, Kuberavāhana stupas, Helor Das, Nokkono Ghwand in Swat)
summary: Further rock-art and inscription studies from the Indus route between Darel/Tangir and Gilgit; context for Xuanzang's route along the Indus gorges.

citation: Hinüber, Oskar von. Die Palola Ṣāhis: Ihre Steininschriften, Inschriften auf Bronzen, Handschriftenkolophone und Schutzzauber. Materialien zur Geschichte von Gilgit und Chilas. Antiquities of Northern Pakistan 5. Mainz: von Zabern, 2004
summary: Edits all inscriptions, bronze dedications and manuscript colophons of the Palola Ṣāhis of Gilgit (c. 600–720, e.g. Hatun inscription of 671/72) and identifies their kingdom with the Chinese Bolu/Bolor (Little Bolor = Gilgit); directly tests 03.02. Leans to Gilgit for Bolor; the study lists 'Baltistan, or Gilgit' (alternative). Heidelberg's bot check blocked the download.

citation: Jettmar, Karl. Beyond the Gorges of the Indus: Archaeology before Excavation. Ed. E. Kattner. Karachi: Oxford University Press, 2002
summary: Jettmar's collected essays on Dardistan, Bolor and the Indus route (incl. 'Bolor and Dardistan' and the Faxian/Xuanzang 'suspended crossing'); synthesis for 03.01.16 and 03.02.

citation: Jettmar, Karl. 'The "suspended crossing": where and why?' In G. Pollet (ed.), India and the Ancient World: History, Trade and Culture before A.D. 650 (Eggermont Festschrift). Orientalia Lovaniensia Analecta 25. Leuven, 1987, 95–101
summary: Locates the hanging-bridge stretch of the Indus (Faxian's 懸度, Xuanzang's route from Darel to Uḍḍiyāna) in the gorges below Darel/Tangir using rock-art stations; supports Darel (03.01.16) as the start of that route.

citation: 土谷遥子 Tsuchiya Haruko. 「『法顕伝』に見える陀歴仏教寺院」 Oriento オリエント 53.1 (2010): 120–
summary: Based on her field surveys in Darel (2003–06), looks for the Buddhist temple of 陀歴 with the wooden Maitreya described by Faxian and Xuanzang (達麗羅). Bears directly on 03.01.16; the PDF is a scan without a text layer, so the site she proposes (Phuguch? see search snippet) still needs reading.

citation: Tsuchiya, Haruko. 'Preliminary report on field research along the ancient routes in the Northern Areas of Pakistan related to the historical Silk Road.' Journal of the Japanese Association for South Asian Studies (Minami Ajia kenkyū) 5 (1993): 1–
summary: Field survey of petroglyph stations and routes between Gilgit, Gakuch/Ishkoman and Darel, incl. the Darel–Gakuch route; context for Xuanzang's Darel and Bolor.

citation: Tsuchiya, Haruko. 'Fa-hsien's route from Pamir to the Darel valley on the Indus: field research in Northern Pakistan 2003–2006.' citation: Hakal, Mueezuddin. 'Faxian's and Xuanzang's Wooden Maitreya and the Chartoi Rock Cut Niche at Gupis, Gilgit-Baltistan.' citation: Wong, Dorothy C. 'Colossal Buddha statues along the Silk Road.' Acta Via Serica 4.2 (2019): 1–27. doi:10.22679/avs.2019.4.2.001

citation: 内記理 Naiki Satoshi. 「玄奘が見たタキシラの都城と仏塔」 (The city and stūpas in Taxila in the time of Xuanzang). Oriento オリエント 64.2 (2021): 217–232

citation: 定方晟 Sadakata Akira. 「タクシラの若干の地名について」 Indogaku Bukkyōgaku kenkyū 印度學佛教學研究 40.1 (1991): 484–

citation: Dani, Ahmad Hasan. The Historic City of Taxila. Paris: UNESCO; Tokyo: Centre for East Asian Cultural Studies, 1986

citation: Fussman, Gérard. 'Taxila: the Central Asian connection.' In H. Spodek and D.M. Srinivasan (eds), Urban Form and Meaning in South Asia. Studies in the History of Art 31. Washington: National Gallery of Art, 1993, 83–100

citation: Kuwayama, Shōshin. 'Pilgrimage route changes and the decline of Gandhāra.' In P. Brancaccio and K. Behrendt (eds), Gandharan Buddhism: Archaeology, Art, Texts. Vancouver: UBC Press, 2006, 107–134

citation: Rienjang, Wannaporn. Honouring the Body: Relic Cult Practice in [Eastern] Afghanistan with Comparison to Dharmarajika[ and Taxila], Pakistan. PhD thesis, University of Cambridge, 2017 [exact subtitle unverified; repository record not found]

citation: Ghafoor, Abdul, Arshad Ullah and Ashraf Khan. 'A Mathuran Style Buddha from Badalpur, Taxila Valley: A Reassessment of the Evidence and New Tentative Dating.' Journal of Asian Civilizations 44, no. 1 (June 2021) [pages not confirmed]

citation: 村上東俊 (Murakami Tōshun), 'ティラウラコットにおける近年の考古学調査について' [The recent archaeological survey of Tilaurakot], 印度學佛教學研究 (Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies) 65(1)

citation: Deeg, Max, Das Gaoseng-Faxian-zhuan als religionsgeschichtliche Quelle: der älteste Bericht eines chinesischen buddhistischen Pilgermönchs über seine Reise nach Indien mit Übersetzung des Textes (Studies in Oriental Religions 52; Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz)

citation: Coningham, R.A.E., K.P. Acharya, C.E. Davis, R.B. Kunwar, et al., 'Geophysical investigations at Ramagrama: results from new surveys undertaken in November 2019 and February 2020', Ancient Nepal (issue no. as listed in Durham record), pp. 5-28

citation: 網干善教・薗田香融・山岡泰造 他, 『祇園精舎: 日・印共同学術調査(1985-89)報告書』 (吹田: 関西大学)

citation: 関西大学文学部考古学研究室, 『インド共和国ウッタル・プラデーシュ州シュラーヴァスティー県所在マヘート遺跡発掘調査概報』 (吹田: 関西大学)

citation: 高橋隆博, 高橋誠一, 木庭元晴, 薮田貫, 中谷伸生, 米田文孝, 山岡泰造, 『インド共和国マヘート(舎衛城)遺跡の研究: 王宮地区の調査』 (KAKEN research report, Kansai University)

citation: Aboshi Yoshinori (PI), 'A study of Maheth (Sravasti) site in India', KAKEN Grant 06041110, final research report summary FY1994-1996
summary: Online summary of the Maheth results: Area A iron working, Area B brick fortification in two phases (c. 250-50 BCE, 50 BCE-100 CE), Kushan well, post-Gupta hall; agrees with Sahet-Mahet = Śrāvastī.

citation: Härtel, Herbert, Excavations at Sonkh: 2500 Years of a Town in Mathura District (Monographien zur indischen Archäologie, Kunst und Philologie 9; Berlin: Dietrich Reimer); open-access reissue CrossAsia-eBooks 2021, doi:10.11588/xabooks.934
summary: German excavation of Sonkh, c. 14 miles from Mathura city (PGW to Jat periods, Kushan apsidal temples); no Buddhist remains and no mention of Xuanzang; the Gupta to early medieval levels show a run-down Hindu settlement (lit_batch16, relevant=no).

citation: Srinivasan, Doris Meth (general ed.), Mathurā: The Cultural Heritage (New Delhi: Manohar Publications for the American Institute of Indian Studies, 1989), xv+405 pp. ISBN 8185054371
summary: Conference volume with papers on Mathura city archaeology (Katra, Govindnagar, Sonkh), its monasteries and inscriptions; context for the Dhulkot rampart city and the monastery sites (bibliographic data from memory).

citation: 仲澤浩祐, '中インドにおけるグプタ期の仏教について: マトゥラー、サンカシャ、カニヤークブジャを中心に', 立正大学大学院紀要
summary: Gupta-period Buddhism at Mathurā, Saṃkāśya and Kanyākubja, using the pilgrims' accounts with the archaeological evidence; agrees with the standard identifications.

citation: Vikram, Bhuvan et al. (ASI Agra Circle), 'Excavation at Ahichchhatra, District Bareilly', Indian Archaeology 2007-08 - A Review (New Delhi: ASI 2016)
summary: First season of the renewed ASI excavation at Ahichchhatra (Ramnagar fort); stratigraphy from PGW; confirms the site, agrees with 04.13 (Xuanzang's nāga-tank stūpa not addressed).

citation: ASI, Indian Archaeology 2009-10 - A Review (New Delhi: ASI 2016): 'Excavations at Ahichchhatra, District Bareilly' and B.R. Mani et al., 'Excavation at Lathiya, District Ghazipur' (no. 38)
summary: Ahichchhatra season continued; Lathiya (Gupta pillar site, c. 20 km SE of Ghazipur) excavated by the Patna Excavation Branch: Early Historic-Gupta settlement in the 戰主國 region (07.02); also conservation notes on Saheth-Maheth.

citation: ASI, Indian Archaeology 2010-11 - A Review (New Delhi: ASI 2016): archaeobotany of Ahichchhatra (Birbal Sahni Institute), and 'Early historical site, Kolhua Chaur, District Muzaffarpur'

citation: ASI, Indian Archaeology 2011-12 - A Review (New Delhi: ASI 2016)
summary: Further archaeobotanical work on the 2009 Ahichchhatra excavation; a conservation note on Sankisa. (Served at the misleading file name 2000-2012.pdf.)

citation: ASI Agra Circle, 'Excavations at Ahichhatra, District Bareilly', Indian Archaeology 2012-13 - A Review, pp. 146-147 (New Delhi: ASI 2015)
summary: Ahichhatra: circular huts and post-holes, adobe structures, gold plaque; the early sequence of the Pañcāla capital (agrees with 04.13). Same volume as mani2016_iar_piprahwa.

citation: Srivastava, K.C. (ASI Excavation Branch Patna), 'Excavation at Lauriya Areraj, District East Champaran', Indian Archaeology 2013-14 - A Review (New Delhi: ASI 2016); same volume has the last Ahichhatra season
summary: Śuṅga-Kushan monastic complex at Lauriya Areraj on the Vaiśālī-Kesariya-Areraj-Lauriya Nandangarh-Rampurwa route north from Vaiśālī: context for Xuanzang's route from Vaiśālī (Kesariya 07.03.13) and for the Pippalivana candidates.

citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Indian Archaeology - A Review, volumes 2006-07, 2007-08, 2009-10, 2010-11, 2011-12, 2012-13, 2013-14 (published 2015-16), hosted by ASI Aurangabad Circle
summary: The post-2001 IAR volumes that are online (2001-06, 2008-09 and 2014- were not found at that address). Text-searchable; 2006-07 has conservation notes on Kushinagar, Sarnath, Vaishali museum, Kesariya stūpa and Thanesar.

citation: Lal, B.B. et al., Kauśāmbī Revisited (New Delhi: Aryan Books International)
summary: Re-examines G.R. Sharma's Kosam dating (rampart, 'palace', Ghositārāma); does not move the city but questions the early chronology (05.05 agrees).

citation: Erdosy, George, Urbanisation in Early Historic India (BAR International Series 430; Oxford: BAR, 1988), iii+211 pp. ISBN 0860545571
summary: Settlement survey of Allahabad district, Kauśāmbī's hinterland and the Prayāga area; site hierarchy for the 憍賞彌國 and 鉢邏耶伽國 regions (series no. from memory).

citation: Maclean, Kama, Pilgrimage and Power: The Kumbh Mela in Allahabad, 1765-1954 (New York: Oxford University Press)
summary: Uses Xuanzang's account of Harṣa's quinquennial assembly and the 'great field of alms' and the temple tree at Prayāga in the history of the Kumbh Mela and the Akshaya Vata; agrees with 05.04.03-04.

citation: Bakker, Hans, Ayodhyā (Groningen Oriental Studies 1; Groningen: Egbert Forsten), 3 parts
summary: History of Ayodhyā-Sāketa from the sources, including the Chinese pilgrims' 沙祇/Viśoka and 阿踰陀; the standard account of Sāketa = Ayodhyā. If Bakker places Xuanzang's 阿踰陀 or 鞞索迦 at Ayodhyā it contradicts the study's Fatehpur-stretch site for 05.02 (check his chapter on the pilgrims).

citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Ayodhya: 2002-03 (excavation report submitted to the Allahabad High Court), 2 vols
summary: Court-ordered excavation at the Ram Janmabhoomi site: early historic to medieval sequence at Ayodhyā; contested; only marginal for Sāketa/Viśoka (05.06).

citation: Gupta, S.P. (ed.), Kushāṇa Sculptures from Sanghol (1st-2nd century A.D.): A Recent Discovery (New Delhi: National Museum)
summary: Publication of the 1985 Sanghol railing hoard and stūpa (SGL-5); evidence for a major Kushan Buddhist centre on the Sutlej plain, relevant to the study's Sanghol candidate for the capital of Śatadru (04.05).

citation: Sanghol and the Archaeology of Punjab (edited volume; includes a chapter by C. Margabandhu on the Sanghol excavations) (New Delhi)
summary: Collected papers on the Sanghol stūpa, the 27-cell monastery and Punjab Buddhist sites (editor and year not verified); bears on 04.05.

citation: Pande, B.M. (dir.) / D.N. Dimri, excavation report on Raja Harsh ka Tila, Thanesar (ASI excavations 1987-88 to 1990-91), submitted to the ASI 2026, unpublished
summary: The long-delayed final report of the Thanesar mound excavation, said to be in press; the only modern stratified data for Sthāneśvara (04.08). Not yet available.

citation: Asher, Frederick M., Sarnath: A Critical History of the Place Where Buddhism Began (Los Angeles: Getty Research Institute)
summary: Critical history of the excavation of Sarnath (Dharmarājika, Dhamekh, Mūlagandhakuṭī, Chaukhandi) and of how the monuments were matched with Xuanzang's description; also on Project MUSE. Agrees with the Sarnath identifications, with caveats on individual monuments.

citation: Li Rongxi (tr.), The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions (BDK English Tripiṭaka 79; Berkeley: Numata Center for Buddhist Translation and Research / BDK America; dBET PDF 2017)
summary: Complete modern English translation of the Xiyu ji (no identifications argued); the free BDK dBET PDF is the official edition.

citation: Singh, Upinder, The Discovery of Ancient India: Early Archaeologists and the Beginnings of Archaeology (Delhi: Permanent Black)
summary: History of how Cunningham and his assistants identified the pilgrims' sites (Kusinagara, Vaiśālī, Kapilavastu, etc.) with Xuanzang as guide; context only.

citation: Verardi, Giovanni, Excavations at Harigaon, Kathmandu: Final Report, 2 vols (IsMEO Reports and Memoirs 25; Rome: IsMEO, 1992)
summary: Italian excavation at Harigaon (Hadigaon), proposed site of the Licchavi palace Kailāsakūṭa-bhavana; relevant to the unidentified capital of 尼波羅國 (07.05) (bibliographic data from memory; check).

citation: Deeg, Max. "Walking the 'Xuanzang Trail' in Bihar – When Text, Archaeology and Landscape Meet". Guest lecture, Institute for Advanced Studies on Asia (東洋文化研究所), University of Tokyo, 26 June 2026; abstract on Glorisun Global Network
summary: Abstract of the project lecture: Xuanzang Trail (Chaudhary and Deeg as PIs), four exploration tours 2020–24 in Magadha and N Bihar, case studies "from Lauriya Nandangarh to Bodhgayā"; names no Magadha site identifications. Lecture-page text, not a publication.

summary: Press release: the team "verified sites mentioned in Xuanzang's record" and "identified previously unknown sites" around Bodhgayā, Nālandā and Rājgir; no site names in the snippets seen (page behind Cloudflare, not read in full). Must be read in a browser.

citation: Cardiff University. "Activating and implementing the Xuanzang Trail project" (community-engagement project page, 2025 projects: heritage walks; posters, maps and booklets on three sites in English and Hindi for the Bihar Museum)

citation: PTI. "Satellite images suggest architectural wealth beneath Mahabodhi temple in Bodh Gaya: Officials". The Week (wire), 13 July 2024 (BHDS–Cardiff project "Archaeology on the footsteps of the Chinese traveller Xuanzang"; M. B. Rajni, NIAS)
summary: Press report of the Xuanzang Trail satellite study: a buried walled square monastery with moat (outer square c. 4.9 acres, inner 2.5) N of the Mahābodhi temple, overlapping the Samanvay Ashram, plus a settlement further N; the Nairañjanā shifted E to W. citation: Deeg, Max (interviewed). "'Xuanzang's work has certain bias that calls for careful interpretation': Max Deeg". The Week, 18 July 2025 (cover story)
summary: Deeg: Telhara, partly excavated by his Xuanzang Trail colleague Bijoy Chaudhury, is the Teladhaka monastery but its excavated plan is "extremely difficult to reconcile" with Xuanzang's neat layout; same caveat for Nālandā's courtyards. Agrees with 08.04.01 (Telhara) while warning against reading the description as a plan.

citation: Choudhary, Bijoy Kumar; Arun Kumar; Oishi Roy; Amit Ranjan. Sri Prathamasivapura Mahavihara: Excavating an Early Medieval Buddhist Monastery at Telhara in Magadh (Eastern India) 2020–2022. Patna: Bihar Heritage Development Society, c. 2023. ISBN 978-81-961222-4-9
