Bears directly on 08.04.01 (Telhara = Teladhaka); the sealing name is a complication the study should note. Publisher details unverified (ISBN only).

citation: Onmanorama (PTI). "Chinese traveller Hiuen Tsang's India visit: Bihar's 2,600-year-old structures to be excavated soon", 11 Dec 2023 (quotes H. K. Bamhrah and Bijoy Kumar Choudhary, BHDS)
summary: BHDS says Xuanzang's sites in South Bihar "have already been discovered" in the Patna–Jehanabad–Gaya–Nawada–Nalanda sector; names none. Press only.

citation: ThePrint (PTI). "BHDS signs MoU with Cardiff University for joint research in archaeology, history, heritage studies", 2022
summary: Announces the BHDS–Cardiff MoU behind the Xuanzang Trail; no sites.

citation: Verma, Atul Kumar. "Telhara (Nalanda) Excavation – A Brief Report". Patna: Directorate of Archaeology, Department of Art, Culture and Youth, Government of Bihar (yac.bih.nic.in), c. 2010–13
summary: State excavation of the Telhara mound from Dec 2009: three-storeyed monastery, Pāla images, over 100 sealings, NBPW and Kushan layers. Confirms 08.04.01 (Telhara = Teladhaka). Original URL dead; Wayback copy offline at time of search, not downloaded.

citation: Sanyal, Rajat. "Discovery of a Buddhist Monastery at Telhara". Monthly Bulletin of the Asiatic Society (Kolkata), 2016
summary: Reads the Telhara monastic sealings (Śrī-Prathamaśivapura-mahāvihāra) and discusses the site's identity with Xuanzang's Teladhaka. Bears on 08.04.01; agrees with Telhara, adds the sealing name.

citation: Biswas, Pampa. "Explored Sculptural Heritage of Telhara, District Nalanda, Bihar: A Recent Visit". Journal of the Directorate of Archaeology & Museums (West Bengal) / Puravritta 1 (2016): 167–183
summary: Survey of loose sculpture at Telhara; supports the site's monastic character, no new locational argument.

citation: Leoshko, Janice. "Buddhist Images from Telhara, a Site in Eastern India". South Asian Studies 4 (1988): 89–97. doi:10.1080/02666030.1988.9628371
summary: Art-historical study of the Telhara images (Pāla), taking Telhara as Xuanzang's Teladhaka. Agrees with 08.04.01.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Ongoing Excavations at Telhada (Telhara)". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 30 Apr 2012
summary: Field report on the 2009– excavation of the "Bāladitya mound" at Telhara and the Teladhaka inscription. Agrees with 08.04.01; note that the excavated mound is called the Baladitya mound (check against the study's "Bulandi mound"). Scholar's blog.

citation: Saran, S. C. "Excavation at Juafardih and its Identification with Kulika". Purātattva 38 (2008): 59–73
summary: ASI Excavation Branch Patna dig (2006–07) of the stūpa mound at Juafardih, c. 2–3 km W/SW of Nālandā: mud stūpa (NBPW) encased in brick (Śuṅga–Kuṣāṇa), disc with Brāhmī "muga"; excavator identifies it with Kolika/Mahāmaudgalyāyana's stūpa. Moves 09.03.08 from "unidentified (Jagdishpur, unconfirmed)" to a published candidate; the study should test it.

citation: Tewari, Rakesh (ed.). "Excavation at Juafardih, District Nalanda". Indian Archaeology 2006–07 – A Review. New Delhi: Archaeological Survey of India (published 2016)
summary: IAR summary of the Juafardih excavation (stūpa, chronology, the "muga" disc). Same claim as Saran 2008: Juafardih = Kolika (09.03.08).

citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Excavation Branch Patna. "Juafardih" (site page; excavation 2006–07, director S. C. Saran; publication Purātattva 38: 59–73)
summary: Official summary: Chalcolithic to 1st–2nd c. CE; mud stūpa erected late in early NBPW, brick casing and pradakṣiṇā path in Śuṅga period; claims it pushes Nālandā's early history back. Supports Juafardih = Kolika (09.03.08). Server refused connections; not read in full.

citation: Archaeological Survey of India, Excavation Branch Patna. "Chandimau" (site page, Lat. 25°03′ N, Long. 85°30′ E)
summary: ASI Excavation Branch site page for Chandimau, Broadley's candidate for Faxian's Nāla / Xuanzang's Kālapināka (09.03.10); content not read (server down). Needs checking: an ASI dig here would test 09.03.10.

citation: Mani, B. R. "Magadha and Mahabharata: Archaeological Indications from Rajgir Area" (conference presentation, uploaded to SlideShare c. 2012)
summary: Summarises Rajgir (Ghosh 1950), Juafardih 2006–07 (C14 dates from the NBPW levels, identified with Kulika) and Ghorakatora near Giriyek 2007–08 (P. K. citation: Anand, Deepak. "Xuanzang and shrines of Sāriputta, Moggallāna and Mahākassapa around Nālandā". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 21 Mar 2024
summary: Kolika = Juafardih (after Saran 2008), with the unexcavated Jagdishpur mound c. 1 km SW as the second (relic) stūpa; Kālapināka = Naṇand rather than Chaṇdimau, with a mound at Shobhāpur as the disciples' stūpa; Indraśailaguhā = Pārbati hill. citation: Anand, Deepak. "Kulika (Xuanzang's Travelogue), Kolit gram (Pali sources)". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), July 2009
summary: Early field reconnaissance plotting Xuanzang's distances from Nālandā and from Naṇand/Chaṇdimau to Kolika; photographs of the Jagdishpur mound, Rukmanisthan and the 2007 Juafardih dig. Bears on 09.03.08. Scholar's blog.

citation: Prasad, Chandra Shekhar. "Nalanda vis-à-vis the Birthplace of Śāriputra". East and West 38, no. 1–4 (1988): 175–188
summary: Argues for Naṇand as Śāriputra's birthplace (Faxian's Nāla, Xuanzang's Kālapināka) and against equating it with Nālandā. Gives a site for 09.03.10, which the study leaves unlocated.

citation: Deeg, Max. "How to Create a Great Monastery: Xuanzang's Foundation Legend of Nālandā in Its Indian Context". Hualin International Journal of Buddhist Studies 3.1 (2020): 228–258. doi:10.15239/hijbs.03.01.07

citation: Asher, Frederick M. Nalanda: Situating the Great Monastery. Mumbai: Marg Foundation, 2015
summary: Survey of Nālandā's excavated remains, sculpture and inscriptions, with discussion of how Xuanzang's and Yijing's descriptions map onto the site (temple row, Sarai mound). Expected to agree with 09.03.01; needed to check the study's readings of 09.03.06, 09.03.x5.

citation: Stewart, Mary L. Nālandā Mahāvihāra: A Study of an Indian Pāla Period Buddhist Site and British Historical Archaeology, 1861–1938. BAR International Series 529. Oxford: BAR, 1989
summary: Historiography and stratigraphic reassessment of the Nālandā excavations, including the use of Xuanzang to label the temple and monastery blocks. Bears on 09.03.01, 09.03.06, 09.03.x4.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Interpreting the travels of Xuanzang from Indraśailaguhā to Īraṇaparvata (Part I) – Kapotaka Monastery". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 22 Aug 2024
summary: Field survey of the Sheikhpura hills: proposes Pachnā hill with Barui village at its N foot (Buddhist images of the 8th–12th c.; mosque on a brick mound) as Kapotaka, c. 45 km from Nālandā, taking Indraśailaguhā = Pārbati. Contradicts the study (Kapotaka and the Avalokiteśvara hill = Parbati; Indraśailaguhā = Giriyek). Scholar's blog.

citation: Tribedy, Elora. "Sinless's Piety: A Recently Recovered Inscribed Image of Vajratārā Maṇḍala from Pachnā Hill, Bihar". Journal of Bengal Art 26 (2021)
summary: Publishes an inscribed Vajratārā maṇḍala image from Pachnā hill, the find Anand (2024) uses to propose Pachnā–Barui as Kapotaka. Bears on 09.03.13 and 09.03.14; the study's Parbati identification should be weighed against it.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Interpreting the travels of Xuanzang from Indraśailaguhā to Īraṇaparvata (Part II) – A big Village south of river Gaṅgā". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 24 Aug 2024
summary: Identifies Xuanzang's large village S of the Ganges with Rajaonā–Chouki–Valgūdar (Lakhisarai), ancient Kṛmilā/Kimbilā, a mound field of c. 200 acres. Contradicts the study (09.03.15a = Shekhpura; Rajaona is the study's Lāvaṇīla 09.03.15b). Scholar's blog.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Interpreting the travels of Xuanzang from Indraśailaguhā to Īraṇaparvata (Part III) – Lāvaṇīla Village". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 25 Aug 2024
summary: Revisits Nōṇgaḍh on the Kiul (Cunningham's Lāvaṇīla stūpa; Asher 2000 agrees): stūpa mound, a second "monastery" mound, yakṣī images found 1961 and 1995, Buddhist images now in Jamui Museum. Argues for Nongarh as Lāvaṇīla, against the study's Rajjana/Rajaona (09.03.15b). Scholar's blog.

citation: Asher, Frederick M. "Sculptures from Rajaona, Valgudar and Jaynagar: Evidence for an Urban Center". East and West 36, no. 1–3 (1986): 227–246
summary: Treats Rajaona–Valgudar–Jaynagar (Lakhisarai) as one early-medieval urban centre (Kṛmilā) with Nongarh as its tīrtha. Bears on 09.03.15a/b; read with the study's Rajaona = Lāvaṇīla.

citation: Asher, Frederick M. "An Image at Lakhi Serai and Its Implications". Artibus Asiae 59, no. 3/4 (2000): 296–302. doi:10.2307/3249882
summary: On a Lakhisarai image, accepting Cunningham's Nongarh as Xuanzang's Lāvaṇīla (p. 302). Disagrees with the study's Rajjana/Rajaona for 09.03.15b.

citation: Bautze-Picron, Claudine. "Lakhi Sarai, an Indian Site of Late Buddhist Iconography and its Position within the Asian Buddhist World". Silk Road Art and Archaeology 2 (1991–92): 239–284
summary: Corpus and interpretation of late Buddhist sculpture from the Lakhisarai sites (Rajaona, Valgudar, Jaynagar, Nongarh). Background for 09.03.15a/b.

citation: Kumar, Anil. "Kṛimilā: A Forgotten Adhiṣṭhāna of Early Medieval Eastern India". Indian Historical Review 38, no. 1 (2011): 23–50
summary: Uses Pāla inscriptions and sculpture to locate the administrative centre Kṛmilā at Rajaona–Valgudar–Jaynagar (Lakhisarai). Bears on 09.03.15a (big village) and 09.03.15b; complicates the study's Shekhpura and Rajaona choices.

citation: Kumar, Anil. "Interesting Early Mediaeval Sculptures of Magadh: A Case Study of Sculptures from 'Krimila Adhisthana'". Proceedings of the Indian History Congress 70 (2009–10): 1034–1048
summary: Newly found sculptures from the Lakhisarai (Kṛmilā) area. Background for 09.03.15a/b.

citation: Kumar, Anil. "Recent Explored Buddhist Monuments at Krimila Adhisthana: Its Implications". In Archaeology of Buddhism: Recent Discoveries in South Asia, 169–181. New Delhi: Manohar, 2016
summary: Explored Buddhist monuments in the Lakhisarai area (Lal Pahari etc.). Bears on the sites E of Indraśailaguhā (09.03.15–15b).

citation: Kumar, Anil. "The Excavated Remains of a Buddhist Nunnery (Matha) at Lal Pahari (Jainagar), District Lakhisarai, Bihar: 2017–18". Bharati (Bulletin of the Dept. of AIHC & Archaeology, BHU) 42 (2018): 107–131
summary: First report of the Visva-Bharati/Bihar Govt. excavation of the hilltop monastery at Lal Pahari, Jainagar (Lakhisarai), with sealings of the Śrīmaddharmavihārika ārya-bhikṣu-saṅgha. New excavated monastery in the zone of 09.03.15/15a/15b; no direct Xuanzang identification known.

citation: Kumar, Anil. "Excavation at Lalpahari (Lakhisarai, Bihar) 2018–2019". In Interrogating Early India: Evolving Perspectives, 26–48. Kolkata, 2019
summary: Second season at Lal Pahari: monastery plan, sealings, ceramics. Same bearing as kumar2018_lalpahari.

citation: Kumar, Anil. "Srimaddharmmavihara – Monastic Sealing from a Recently Excavated Buddhist Site in South Bihar". Monthly Bulletin of the Asiatic Society (Kolkata) 53, no. 5 (2024): 45–49
summary: Reads the Lal Pahari monastic sealing (Śrīmad-dharma-vihāra). Gives the excavated monastery's own name; useful in testing any Xuanzang identification near Lakhisarai.

citation: Kumar, Anil. "Krimila: A Forgotten Nagar of Early Medieval Eastern India". NMML Occasional Paper. New Delhi: Nehru Memorial Museum and Library, 2019: 1–35
summary: Updated synthesis on Kṛmilā (Rajaona–Valgudar–Jaynagar–Lal Pahari). Bears on 09.03.15a/b.

citation: Kumar, Anil. "Locating 'Chaliya Parvat', A Forgotten Stupa: As Centre of Shared Culture and Different Histories in Early India". Dharmadoot 81 (2015): 62–79
summary: Locates a forgotten stūpa ("Chaliya Parvat") in south Bihar; whether it bears on a Xuanzang site in juan 9 not checked.

citation: Chattopadhyay, R. K.; K. Bandyopadhyay. "Archaeology of Nongarh: A Reconnaissance". History Today (New Delhi) 18 (2017)
summary: Reconnaissance of the Nongarh mounds (Cunningham's Lāvaṇīla stūpa). Bears on 09.03.15b; the study's Rajaona choice should be tested against it.

citation: Bandyopadhyay, K. K.; R. K. Chattopadhyay; S. Majumder. "Recent Study of Sculptural and Architectural Remains from the South Bihar Plain: A Case Study of Rajaonā-Chowki Region". Journal of Bengal Art 20 (2015): 205–228
summary: Documents the sculpture and architecture of Rajaona–Chowki (Gupta to Pāla). Bears on the study's Rajaona = Lāvaṇīla (09.03.15b) and on 09.03.15a.

citation: Chattopadhyay, R. K.; Rajat Sanyal. "Contexts and Contents of Early Historic Sites in the South Bihar Plains: An Archaeological Perspective". In Archaeology of Early Historic South Asia, ed. G. Sengupta and S. Chakraborty, 247–280. New Delhi: Pragati, 2008
summary: Regional survey of early historic sites in the S Bihar plains (Lakhisarai, Sheikhpura, Nalanda districts). Background for the juan 9 sites E of Nālandā.

citation: Chakrabarti, Dilip K. Archaeological Geography of the Ganga Plain: The Lower and the Middle Ganga. Delhi: Permanent Black, 2001
summary: District-by-district site gazetteer for Bihar from the author's surveys (e.g. the Nongarh yakṣī finds, pp. 173–174). Needed to check sites around the study's identifications in Patna, Nalanda, Gaya, Lakhisarai.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Tapassu, Bhallika and Kassapa Brothers – Shrines and Stūpas south of Mahābodhi Temple". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 20 Mar 2024
summary: Field survey S of Bodh Gayā with drone imagery: Muchalinda = Mochārim; Tapassu–Bhallika shrine = Gothu mound; the conversion of the Kassapa brothers = Khajawati (W bank, 1 km S of Kāzichak); other mounds at Kāzichak, Babhani, Shivrājpur. 08.06.18 agrees with one of the study's open options (Muchharin); 08.06.x4 contradicts the study (Urel, Cunningham). Scholar's blog.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Ratanāgiri Rock: The place where Siddhārtha ate food offered by Sujātā". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 10 Jan 2019
summary: Questions the conventional Sujātā/Mātaṅgavāpī/Dharmāraṇya identifications E of the Nairañjanā and uses the 1973 ASI dig of the Bakraur mound to argue for the austerity sites around Bakraur. Bears on 09.01.01 (Bakraur stūpa), which it agrees is the Bakraur mound. Scholar's blog.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "On an Expedition to Locate the Site of Uddaka Rāmaputta's Hermitage". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 22 Mar 2024
summary: Takes the river E of the Mohana as the Paimār and proposes Gāfā Kalān or Nāmā (Nāmā Dih mound, broken Buddhist images) on the Paimār, c. 6 km from Bakraur, as Udraka Rāmaputra's hermitage; no pillar found. Gives candidates for 09.01.02, which the study leaves unidentified. Scholar's blog.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Walking the Buddha Trail along the Prāgbodhi, Jeṭhian and Rājgir Hills". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 24 Jan 2021
summary: Walking narrative; notes that Prāgbodhi (Dhongra/Dungeshwari) rests on circumstantial evidence only, and records the Silāo Kāśyapa inscription. Agrees with 08.05.03.

citation: Deeg, Max. "The Centre of Centres: Bodhgayā in Chinese Sources". Seminar (New Delhi) 745 (Sept 2021)
summary: Reviews Faxian, Xuanzang, Yijing and the Song Chinese steles from Bodhgayā (mid-9th c. to 1033) on the Mahābodhi temple and its monasteries, including the Sri Lankan Mahābodhi saṅghārāma. Bears on 08.06.30 and 08.06.04; no new location.

citation: Deeg, Max. "Donations to the Centre of the World: The Chinese Inscriptions from Bodhgaya". Lecture, Center for Buddhist Studies, University of Arizona, 9 Apr 2024 (also given as "Stones and Chisels for the Buddha", Glorisun lecture series)
summary: Lecture announcement: re-study of the Song Chinese steles Cunningham found at Bodhgayā, recovered from the Indian Museum, Kolkata. Indirect bearing on the Mahābodhi precinct.

citation: Amar, Abhishek Singh. "Buddhist Responses to Brāhmaṇa Challenges in Medieval India: Bodhgayā and Gayā". Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, 3rd ser., 22, no. 1 (2012): 155–185
summary: Studies the relationship of Buddhist Bodhgayā and Brahmanical Gayā (Gayāśīrṣa, Brahmayoni, the tīrthas) using inscriptions and texts. Bears on 08.05.01/08.05.01a; agrees with Brahmayoni/Gayā town as far as known.

citation: Geary, David; Matthew R. Sayers; Abhishek Singh Amar (eds.). Cross-Disciplinary Perspectives on a Contested Buddhist Site: Bodh Gaya Jataka. London: Routledge, 2012
summary: Collected essays (archaeology, art history, history, anthropology) on Bodh Gayā, including Amar on the sacred geography of Bodhgayā and Asher on the temple. Bears on the Mahābodhi precinct (08.06.01, 08.06.04, 08.06.30).

citation: Geary, David. The Rebirth of Bodh Gaya: Buddhism and the Making of a World Heritage Site. Seattle: University of Washington Press, 2017
summary: Modern history and heritage-making of Bodh Gayā; little bearing on locating Xuanzang's sites.

citation: Leoshko, Janice (ed.). Bodhgaya, the Site of Enlightenment. Bombay: Marg Publications, 1988
summary: Essays on the Mahābodhi temple, railing and sculpture, with discussion of the early pilgrim accounts. Bears on 08.06.01, 08.06.04.

citation: Kinnard, Jacob N. Places in Motion: The Fluid Identities of Temples, Images, and Pilgrims. New York: Oxford University Press, 2014
summary: Shared Buddhist/Hindu claims on Bodh Gayā and its images; no bearing on locations.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Curious Case of Mahākassapa Skeleton at Gurpā". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 25 Jan 2024
summary: Revisits R. D. Banerji's 1906 identification of Gurpā hill as Kukkuṭapādagiri and the skeleton reported from its tank. Agrees with 09.01.03 (Gurpa). Scholar's blog.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Gurupāda / Kukkutapāda Giri / Cockfoot's Mountain, and the Maitreya Buddha". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 2 Jan 2011
summary: Reviews Cunningham (Kurkihar), Stein (Hasra Kol) and Banerji (Gurpa) and accepts Gurpā hill (25°32′57″ N, 85°18′13″ E as printed). Agrees with 09.01.03. Scholar's blog.

citation: Mitchell, M. "Following Faxian to Kāśyapa's Gate: Relocating India in the 1692 Jizu shanzhi". MA thesis, University of British Columbia, 2022
summary: How the Chinese Jizu shan (Yunnan) gazetteer re-sited Kukkuṭapāda in China using Faxian and Xuanzang. Reception history, not the Indian location of 09.01.03. (PDF download did not return a PDF.)

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Discovery of Buddhavana". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 11 Jul 2012
summary: Proposes the cave hill at Ayer (Ayer-Pathri, 24°55′18″ N, 85°14′22″ E), 9 km W of Jethian in the same valley, as Buddhavana: cave with brick stūpas, votive stūpa fragments, inscribed images, a mound at the foot; rejects Cunningham and Stein. Gives a site for 09.02.01, which the study leaves unidentified; keeps Jethian = Yaṣṭivana. Scholar's blog with field evidence.

citation: Anand, Deepak. "Pipphali Cave, Rāhula Stūpa and other Forgotten shrines of Rājagṛiha". Nālandā – Insatiable in Offering (blog), 19 Jan 2021
summary: Prefers Marshall's site at the foot of Vaibhāra for the Saptaparṇī hall over Beglar's cave (agrees with 09.02.16). Takes the Pippala cave as the cave Broadley cleared, not the room in the Jarāsandh-kā-baiṭhak platform (fits 09.02.11a's cave behind the platform). Scholar's blog.

citation: Falk, Harry. Aśokan Sites and Artefacts: A Source-Book with Bibliography. Monographien zur indischen Archäologie, Kunst und Philologie 18. Mainz: Philipp von Zabern, 2006
summary: Site-by-site handbook of Aśokan sites with literature (Barābar caves, Bodh Gayā, Pāṭaliputra/Kumrahar, Rājgir). Reference for 08.02.05, 08.04.02 and other Aśokan monuments Xuanzang names.

citation: Deeg, Max. Das Gaoseng-Faxian-Zhuan als religionsgeschichtliche Quelle: Der älteste Bericht eines chinesischen buddhistischen Pilgermönchs über seine Reise nach Indien mit Übersetzung des Textes. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 2005
summary: Annotated translation of Faxian with notes on the Magadha stations Xuanzang also describes (Nāla, the Indraśailaguhā, Rājagṛha, Kukkuṭapāda). Parallel evidence for many juan 9 identifications.

citation: Deeg, Max. "'Show Me the Land Where the Buddha Dwelled…': Xuanzang's 'Record of the Western Regions' (Xiyu ji): A Misunderstood Text?". China Report 48, no. 1–2 (2012): 89–113
summary: Method: argues the Xiyu ji is a court-oriented text whose distances and descriptions must not be read naively as an itinerary. Relevant to the study's use of li figures in general.

citation: Li Rongxi (trans.). The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions. BDK English Tripiṭaka 79. Berkeley: Numata Center for Buddhist Translation and Research, 1996
summary: Standard modern English translation (no locational notes); used by Anand and others as the text of reference.

citation: 董志翘 (Dong Zhiqiao) 譯注. 《大唐西域記》. 中華經典名著全本全注全譯叢書. 北京: 中華書局, 2012
summary: Modern Chinese annotated translation; notes largely follow Ji Xianlin 1985 on Magadha place identifications.

citation: Alam, Md. Shafiqul & Jean-François Salles (eds.), France-Bangladesh Joint Venture Excavations at Mahasthangarh: First Interim Report 1993–1999. Dhaka: Department of Archaeology, Ministry of Cultural Affairs, 2001. 495 pp.
summary: Stratified sequence for the walled city of Mahasthangarh (Mauryan to medieval); the archaeological basis for Mahasthan = Puṇḍranagara, the Puṇḍravardhana capital. Agrees with the study (10.04). Second volume (Dhaka 2017, 228 pp.) catalogued at zenon 001549729.

citation: Salles, Jean-François (ed.), Mahasthan II: Fouilles du rempart Est. Études archéologiques. Archaeologies of the Indian Ocean 10. Turnhout: Brepols, 2015. 438 pp.
summary: Final report on the French–Bangladeshi excavation of the east rampart of Mahasthangarh (1993–2011 mission); dates the fortification and occupation sequence of the city. Supports the study's Mahasthan capital (10.04); a third volume on 2001–11 work was announced.

citation: Rahman, Shah Sufi Mostafizur, Archaeological Investigation in Bogra District (from Early Historic to Early Mediaeval Period). Studies in Bengal Art Series 3. Dhaka: International Centre for Study of Bengal Art, 2000. 300 pp. ISBN 9848140018
summary: Survey and gazetteer of the sites around Mahasthan, including Vasu Vihara/Bhasu Vihar (Narapatir Dhap) excavated by the Bangladesh Department of Archaeology (1970s–80s). Needed for the Bhasu Vihar = 跋始婆 identification (10.04.02); Banglapedia notes the excavated levels are 10th–11th c. and do not reach Xuanzang's period, a weakness for the study's 'strengthened' rating.

citation: Chakrabarti, Dilip K., Ancient Bangladesh: A Study of the Archaeological Sources. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1992.
summary: Archaeological geography of Bangladesh: Mahasthan and its satellite sites (incl. Bhasu Bihar), the Lalmai–Mainamati ridge and Samataṭa, and the old courses of the Karatoya/Brahmaputra. Supports Mahasthan for Puṇḍravardhana and the Comilla region for Samataṭa.

citation: Chakrabarti, Dilip K., Archaeological Geography of the Ganga Plain: The Lower and the Middle Ganga. Delhi: Permanent Black, 2001.
summary: Field survey of the early historic sites along the Ganga from Bihar to Bengal: Munger and Lakhisarai hills (Uren), Champanagar/Bhagalpur and Kahalgaon, the Rajmahal–Teliagarhi gap (Kajaṅgala), Rajbadidanga/Karnasuvarna. Tests the 19th-c. identifications on the ground; generally consistent with the study's Monghyr, Champanagar, Rajmahal and Rangamati identifications.

citation: Chakrabarti, Dilip K., Archaeology of Eastern India: Chhotanagpur Plateau and West Bengal. Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal, 1993.
summary: Regional synthesis covering Tamluk and the coastal sites and the Rajbadidanga (Raktamṛttikā) excavation with its monastic sealing; supports Tamluk (10.07) and Rangamati/Rajbadidanga (10.08, 10.08.02).

citation: Kumar, Anil, 'Srimaddharmmavihara: Monastic Sealing from a Recently Excavated Buddhist Site in South Bihar', Monthly Bulletin of the Asiatic Society (Kolkata) 53 [LIII], no. 5 (2024): 45–49
summary: Publishes the sealing 'Śrīmaddharmavihāra' from the Visva-Bharati/Bihar Heritage Development Society excavation (2017–21) of the hilltop monastery at Lal Pahari, Lakhisarai (ancient Kṛmilā). New monastic evidence in the Monghyr–Lakhisarai hill country of Īraṇaparvata (10.01; cf. Uren 10.01.04); the excavators link the area with Xuanzang's hill monasteries. Does not move the Monghyr capital.

citation: Datta, Asok, Excavations at Moghalmari: First Interim Report (2003-04 to 2007-08). Kolkata: The Asiatic Society, 2008.
summary: Large 6th–8th c. stuccoed monastery at Moghalmari (Paschim Medinipur), in Tāmraliptī's hinterland; later seasons (to 2012) yielded inscribed sealings naming monasteries. Shows the kind of monastery Xuanzang counted (10 in Tāmraliptī) but does not alter Tamluk as the capital (10.07).

citation: Imam, Abu, Excavations at Mainamati: An Exploratory Study. Dhaka: International Centre for Study of Bengal Art, 2000.
summary: Critical review of the Mainamati–Lalmai excavations (Shalban Vihara, Ananda Vihara, Kotila Mura, palace mound) and their 7th–8th c. Deva-period chronology. Bears on whether the 7th-c. Samataṭa capital was on the ridge (Devaparvata) or at Bad-Kamta (Karmānta) as the study prefers.

citation: Rashid, M. Harunur, The Early History of South-East Bengal in the Light of Archaeological Material. Dhaka: Itihas Academy, 2008. xiii+266 pp.
summary: Synthesis by the long-time excavator of Mainamati of the coins, copper plates and sealings from Lalmai–Mainamati; discusses the successive capitals of Samataṭa (Karmānta-vāsaka/Bad-Kamta and Devaparvata). Directly relevant to the study's Bad-Kamta capital (10.06).

citation: Furui, Ryosuke, Land and Society in Early South Asia: Eastern India 400–1250 AD. London/New York: Routledge, 2020.
summary: Epigraphic history of Puṇḍravardhana, Samataṭa and Gauḍa/Karṇasuvarṇa based on copper plates (incl. 6th–7th c. grants from Samataṭa and Śaśāṅka's Karṇasuvarṇa); useful for the administrative geography behind 10.04, 10.06, 10.08. No change to the identifications.

citation: Lahiri, Nayanjot, Pre-Ahom Assam: Studies in the Inscriptions of Assam between the Fifth and the Thirteenth Centuries AD. Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal, 1991.
summary: Uses the Varman inscriptions (Bhāskaravarman's Nidhanpur and Dubi plates) for the extent of Kāmarūpa and its western border; relevant to the capital at Prāgjyotiṣa/Guwahati and to the Karatoya as the river crossed (10.05, 10.05.x1). Consistent with the study.

citation: Prusty, Harish Chandra & Pradeep Mohanty, 'Langudi: A Unique Rock-cut Buddhist Site in Orissa', Bulletin of the Deccan College Research Institute 53 (1993): 325–327. JSTOR 42936452.
summary: First report of the Langudi hill (Jajpur district) site; later OIMSEAS/Odisha State excavations (1996–2006) found inscriptions read 'puṣpa sabhar giriya' and the excavators identified Langudi with Puṣpagiri. Contradicts the study's Udayagiri–Khandagiri (Bhubaneswar) identification of 10.09.02 and moves Puṣpagiri to the Jajpur group (Langudi/Lalitgiri/Ratnagiri/Udayagiri).

citation: Pradhan, Debraj [and colleagues], reports on the Langudi hill excavations (Kayama/Deuli/Langudi, Jajpur), Orissa Institute of Maritime and South East Asian Studies / Odisha State Archaeology, c. 1996–2006 (incl. inscribed stupa fragments read as Aśokan). [exact titles to verify]
summary: The excavation reports behind the Langudi = Puṣpagiri identification (inscriptions naming the hill; stupa with image identified as Aśoka). Contradicts the study's Udayagiri–Khandagiri identification of 10.09.02; B.N. Mukherjee disputed the Aśoka reading. Bibliographic details still to be pinned down. An earlier publication: Prusty & Mohanty,]

citation: Patnaik, Jeeban Kumar, Excavations at Lalitagiri (1985–1991). Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 112. New Delhi: ASI, 2016. xxi+390 pp.
summary: Final report on the ASI excavation of Lalitgiri (stūpa with relic caskets, apsidal caitya, four monasteries, 1st–13th c.). Long cited as a Puṣpagiri candidate; the report gives no epigraphic proof of the name. Bears on 10.09.02 as an alternative to the study's Udayagiri–Khandagiri.

citation: Bandyopadhyay, Bimal, Excavations at Udayagiri-2 (1997–2000). Memoirs of the ASI 100. New Delhi: ASI, 2007. xiii+155 pp.
summary: Excavation of the Jajpur Udayagiri monastery (Mādhavapura Mahāvihāra by its sealings). Note: this Udayagiri is the Jajpur (Assia hills) site, not the Bhubaneswar hill paired with Khandagiri in the study's 10.09.02a; the report is the evidence for that alternative.

citation: Trivedi, P. K., Further Excavations at Udayagiri-2, Odisha (2001–03). Memoirs of the ASI 104. New Delhi: ASI, 2012. xviii + 352 pp.
summary: Further seasons at the Jajpur Udayagiri (stūpa, monasteries, sealings). Relevant to whether Xuanzang's 'NW mountain monastery' and Puṣpagiri lie in the Jajpur group rather than at Bhubaneswar (study 10.09.02/10.09.02a).

citation: Archaeological Survey of India (Puri Circle / Excavation Branch), renewed excavation at Ratnagiri, Jajpur, from December 2024 (colossal Buddha heads, monolithic elephant, monastic and caitya-gṛha structures, 7th–14th c. pottery). Press reports only; no report yet.
summary: First ASI work at Ratnagiri since Debala Mitra (1958–61). ASI officials suggest Xuanzang may have visited Ratnagiri; nothing published yet that tests Puṣpagiri or the Oḍra capital. Watch for IAR/ASI report.

citation: Patnaik, Sunil Kumar, 'Archaeology of Early Historic Site of Radhanagar, Jajpur District, Odisha: A Fresh Appraisal', Heritage: Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies in Archaeology 10 (2022–23): 363–384.
summary: Summarises the 2010–13 excavation of the fortified city of Radhanagar (with the Langudi Buddhist sites nearby), proposed as Aśoka's Tosali and by some as Dantapura, capital of Kaliṅga; lists coastal Buddhist sites from Tamralipti to Amaravati incl. Dantapura and Kalingapatnam. A Radhanagar = Dantapura view would put the old Kaliṅga capital in Oḍra, not S of Ganjam; it concerns the early historic period, not Xuanzang's 7th-c. capital (10.11 still open).

citation: Singh, Upinder, Kings, Brāhmaṇas and Temples in Orissa: An Epigraphic Study AD 300–1147. Delhi: Munshiram Manoharlal, 1994.
summary: Epigraphic historical geography of Oḍra/Toṣalī, the Śailodbhava Koṅgoda-maṇḍala and the Eastern Gaṅga Kaliṅga (Kaliṅganagara = Mukhalingam). Background for the study's Koṅgoda (10.10) and the open Kaliṅga capital (10.11).

citation: Tripathy, Snigdha, Inscriptions of Orissa, vol. I: Circa Fifth–Eighth Centuries A.D. Delhi: Indian Council of Historical Research & Motilal Banarsidass, 1997. ISBN 8120810775
summary: Corpus of 5th–8th c. Odishan copper plates incl. the Śailodbhava grants issued from Koṅgoda and the early Gaṅga grants from Kaliṅganagara; the primary evidence for locating Koṅgoda's capital and the 7th-c. Kaliṅga capital (10.10, 10.11).

citation: Donaldson, Thomas E., Iconography of the Buddhist Sculpture of Orissa. 2 vols. New Delhi: IGNCA & Abhinav, 2001.
summary: Site-by-site survey of Odishan Buddhist sites (Lalitgiri, Ratnagiri, Udayagiri, Langudi etc.) with a discussion of the Puṣpagiri problem; dating of the Jajpur sites relative to Xuanzang's visit.

citation: Sharma, A.K., Prabhat Kumar Singh and Praveen Tirkey, Excavations at Sirpur 2000–2012: Antiquities. New Delhi: Aayu Publications, 2017. xiv+181 pp. ISBN 9789385161513
summary: Large-scale excavation of the Pāṇḍuvaṃśī capital Śrīpura: palace, many monasteries (Ānandaprabhakuṭī etc.), temples, 6th–8th c. Confirms Sirpur as a major 7th-c. capital with active Buddhist monasteries; agrees with the study (10.12). Sharma's stratigraphy and dating have been criticised.

citation: Shastri, Ajay Mitra, Inscriptions of the Śarabhapurīyas, Pāṇḍuvaṃśins and Somavaṃśins. 2 vols. Delhi: ICHR & Motilal Banarsidass, 1995.
summary: Edition of the Dakṣiṇa Kosala inscriptions incl. the Sirpur Buddhist inscriptions and place names around Arang; basis for Śrīpura as capital (10.12) and for any local name behind Bhramaragiri (10.12.05).

citation: Stone, Elizabeth Rosen, The Buddhist Art of Nāgārjunakoṇḍa. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.
summary: Monograph on Nāgārjunakoṇḍa (Vijayapurī), the site Mizutani and others proposed for Bhramaragiri/Śrīparvata; its 3rd–4th c. date and location in Andhra (not Kosala) tell against that identification, consistent with the study's local alternative.

citation: Shimada, Akira, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context: The Great Stūpa at Amarāvatī (ca. 300 BCE–300 CE). Brill's Indological Library 43. Leiden: Brill, 2013. Open access (OAPEN).
summary: Archaeological and epigraphic study of Amarāvatī and Dharanikota (Dhānyakaṭaka): the stūpa's setting relative to the walled city, the sect affiliations (Pūrvaśaila/Aparaśaila inscriptions in the region). Supports the study's Dharanikota capital and Amaravati = Pūrvaśaila (10.14, 10.14.02a); argues Amarāvatī was not merely a suburb of Dharanikota.

citation: Shimada, Akira & Michael Willis (eds.), Amaravati: The Art of an Early Buddhist Monument in Context. British Museum Research Publication 207. London: British Museum, 2016.
summary: Essays on the Amarāvatī stūpa, its excavation history, coins (Bhandare on Sada coins from Dharanikota) and the history of Dhānyakaṭaka. Context for 10.14; no change to the identification.

citation: Griffiths, Arlo, Vincent Tournier & Akira Shimada (eds.), Early Āndhradeśa: Historical Studies around the Epigraphic Corpus. 2 vols (I: Inventory; II: Studies). Gonda Indological Studies 25. Leiden: Brill, 2025. Open access. [held: vol. II (Studies) only, the whole open-access volume from Brill, 678 pp.; vol. I (Inventory) still wanted]
summary: Inventory and re-edition of >1000 early Andhra inscriptions (EIAD corpus) and eleven studies on the political and religious geography of Āndhra (Dhānyakaṭaka, Veṅgī, the Śaila sects). The new primary reference for 10.13–10.15; Brill blocks scripted download, fetch the PDF by hand.

citation: Deeg, Max (with an appendix by Peter Zieme), 'Chinese Reports about Buddhism in Early Āndhra', in Griffiths, Tournier & Shimada (eds.), Early Āndhradeśa, vol. II. Leiden: Brill, 2025, pp. 565–591. DOI 10.1163/9789004744097_015. Open access (CC BY-NC).
summary: Re-reads Xuanzang's and other Chinese accounts of Āndhra and Dhānyakaṭaka (Pūrvaśaila/Avaraśaila, the Asura palace hill) against the epigraphic evidence; the most recent Xuanzang-specific treatment of 10.13–10.14. Repository blocked scripted download; fetch by hand.
